Demo letters are house-written in the voice of an invented author and marked demo. Classics letters are written by Akana about the author, never in the dead author's voice. Shape: TitleCopy in packages/schema/src/v3.ts. Checked by pnpm validate.

titles.card_line: Keep a cash book you will actually use, and know what each day brought in.
titles.end_state: By week six you will have a one-page daily cash book and a weekly count that you trust. You will know what each line of stock costs you and what it leaves behind. You will also have set money aside for stock, rent and slow months, so a quiet week no longer catches you out. All of it fits on paper you can keep behind the till.
who_for: Traders who keep their own books on scraps of paper
Shop owners who never quite know what the week brought in
Anyone who wants a routine that takes ten minutes a day

letters.title: A welcome from Chidinma Obiora-Lane
letters.body: {first_name}, welcome. Years ago I kept my stall takings in my head and in a pocket. This workbook is the plan I wish I had been given. Ten minutes a day is enough. Start with the cash book and the rest builds on it.

letters.title: A note for week 2
letters.body: {first_name}, you are about to work out costs and margins. Do not worry if a few numbers surprise you. Most traders find one or two. Write them down and carry on to the next line of stock.

letters.title: A note for week 4
letters.body: {first_name}, this is the week to set money aside. Pick an amount that feels almost too small. A small amount kept every week is worth more than a large one promised and then dropped.

letters.title: A note for week 6
letters.body: {first_name}, you have kept a book for six weeks. Keep the daily page and the weekly count going. Next time you want to change a price, the numbers will be there to look at first.

titles.card_line: Know your regulars by name and give them a fair reason to come back.
titles.end_state: At the end you will have a written list of your regular customers, with what each one usually buys and when they were last in. You will have a short routine for following up after a sale and a plain way to deal with a complaint. You will also have two or three offers you are happy to stand behind, and a note of which ones brought people back. The list lives in a notebook you already own.
who_for: Shop owners who rely on repeat trade
Stallholders who know faces but forget names
Anyone who wants to follow up without feeling pushy

letters.title: A welcome from Chidinma Obiora-Lane
letters.body: {first_name}, welcome. In my two shops the best customers were never the loudest. They were the ones who came back on Thursday. This workbook helps you notice who they are, and thank them properly.

letters.title: A note for week 2
letters.body: {first_name}, a good list takes patience. Keep adding names this week, even half a name and a purchase. By the end of the month the notebook will tell you things your memory misses.

letters.title: A note for week 4
letters.body: {first_name}, complaints arrive in every shop. This week is about answering them calmly and fairly. Listen to the whole story first. Then offer what you can honestly give, and write down what happened.

letters.title: A note for week 6
letters.body: {first_name}, you are asking for referrals now. Keep it light. A friendly word at the counter works better than a speech. Choose one regular today and ask.

letters.title: A note for week 8
letters.body: {first_name}, thank you for finishing. Look back over the notebook and mark the offers that brought people back. Keep those and drop the rest. The list is yours to keep adding to.

titles.card_line: Take orders by message and send them out, with one stock count for shop and online.
titles.end_state: You will have one online channel chosen and set up, with photographs of your best lines taken in a way you can repeat. You will have a written routine for taking an order, receiving payment and sending the goods out, so each sale follows the same steps. You will also have a single stock count that covers both the stall and the online shop. You stop selling things you no longer have.
who_for: Small shop owners starting to sell online
Stallholders who take orders by message already
Anyone who wants one stock count, not two

letters.title: A welcome from Chidinma Obiora-Lane
letters.body: {first_name}, welcome. Selling online does not mean building a website this month. It means choosing one place, photographing your stock well and taking orders in a steady way. Begin with a single channel.

letters.title: A note for week 2
letters.body: {first_name}, photographs are done. This week is the order routine. Write the steps down in the order you do them, payment and delivery included. A printed card by your phone saves a great many mistakes.

letters.title: A note for week 4
letters.body: {first_name}, you are now running two places to sell. Count stock once, in one book, at the same time each week. That single habit prevents most of the trouble.

letters.title: A note for week 6
letters.body: {first_name}, thank you for working through this. Keep the order card and the stock count in use. Add a second channel later, once the first feels ordinary.

titles.card_line: Run a listening round each week and make decisions people can follow.
titles.end_state: Over twelve weeks you will have a regular listening round for your team and a notebook of what you heard. You will have a plain way to decide in the open: the question, the options, the choice and the reason. You will also have named two or three people you are growing to lead, with a first piece of real authority handed to each. It is a leader's habit written down, not a theory.
who_for: Leaders who want to hear their team before deciding
Managers taking on a bigger group
People asked to grow others and unsure where to begin

letters.title: A welcome from Efua Dadzie-Lamptey
letters.body: {first_name}, welcome. Among the cocoa farmers, a meeting was not over until the quietest person had spoken. This workbook asks you to build that habit. Begin with listening and take notes.

letters.title: A note for week 3
letters.body: {first_name}, you have listened for three weeks. Look at your notes. Who has not spoken yet? Be patient and ask them directly, in private if that suits them better.

letters.title: A note for week 6
letters.body: {first_name}, halfway through, take a morning to read the whole notebook. Patterns appear that no single week shows. Next you decide in the open: give the choice and the reason in plain words.

letters.title: A note for week 9
letters.body: {first_name}, handing over authority is the hardest part. Start with something small and real, and say clearly that the decision is theirs. Then keep your hands off it.

letters.title: A note for week 12
letters.body: {first_name}, thank you for twelve weeks. A good leader leaves things better after leaving the room. Keep the listening round going and choose who you will grow next.

titles.card_line: Meet each person on your new team and agree how you will work together.
titles.end_state: By the end of six weeks you will have met each person on your team one to one. You will have written down what each of them needs from you. You will have agreed roles, goals and a simple rhythm of check-ins. You will also have given your first piece of feedback and run a short team review. All of it sits in one notebook that you can show to your own manager.
who_for: People in their first weeks as a manager
Team leads promoted from the same team
Anyone who wants a clear first month and a half

letters.title: A welcome from Efua Dadzie-Lamptey
letters.body: {first_name}, welcome to your first team. Most new managers try to prove themselves quickly. A better start is to listen. This workbook gives you six weeks of small, practical steps.

letters.title: A note for week 2
letters.body: {first_name}, you have met everyone. Now agree roles and goals together. Write them in plain words and share the page. People work more steadily when they can see what is expected.

letters.title: A note for week 4
letters.body: {first_name}, feedback conversations come next. Choose something specific you saw and say it kindly. Then ask for their view. A short, honest conversation beats a long, careful one.

letters.title: A note for week 6
letters.body: {first_name}, thank you for the work so far. Close with a team review that everyone helps to write. Keep the notebook. It will be useful again when the team changes.

titles.card_line: List what only you can do, then hand the rest on with clear checkpoints.
titles.end_state: You will finish with a written list of what only you can do and what others could take on. You will have briefed at least one task properly, agreed checkpoints and stepped back while it was done. You will also have a short review of what changed and a list of the next things to hand over. The list becomes your plan for the coming quarter, not a one-off exercise.
who_for: Hands-on leaders who still do most things themselves
Owners who cannot take a full day off
Managers who want to delegate without losing track

letters.title: A welcome from Efua Dadzie-Lamptey
letters.body: {first_name}, welcome. Letting go of the clipboard is hard, because you do the work well. This workbook is four weeks long and starts with an honest list. Write down everything you do in a week.

letters.title: A note for week 2
letters.body: {first_name}, now brief a task. Say what good looks like, by when and who to ask. Agree the checkpoints before you walk away. Then keep to them and resist the urge to take it back.

letters.title: A note for week 3
letters.body: {first_name}, this is the week to look back. Ask the person what they found hard. Their answers are often the most useful part of the whole exercise.

letters.title: A note for week 4
letters.body: {first_name}, thank you for finishing. Choose the next task to hand over and put a date next to it. A list of intentions does little. A dated one gets done.

titles.card_line: Write group rules everyone agrees to, keep clear records and plan payouts without arguments.
titles.end_state: You will have a written set of group rules covering contributions, roles and what happens when someone is late. You will have a simple record book and a monthly report that every member can read. You will also have a plan for payouts and a calm way to handle a dispute before it grows. Members sign the rules together, so the group runs on what it agreed, not on memory.
who_for: Members and officers of savings groups
Anyone about to start a group with friends or neighbours
Treasurers who want tidier books

letters.title: A welcome from Wanjiru Kamau-Otieno
letters.body: {first_name}, welcome. In the savings evenings I run, trouble almost always comes from rules that were never written down. This workbook starts there. Put the rules on paper and read them aloud together.

letters.title: A note for week 2
letters.body: {first_name}, records come next. Write every contribution on the day it is paid and give a receipt. The book is dull to keep. It is also what makes everyone trust the group.

letters.title: A note for week 4
letters.body: {first_name}, late payments will happen. Decide in advance what the group does, and apply it the same way to everyone. Fairness is worth more than speed.

letters.title: A note for week 6
letters.body: {first_name}, thank you for the care you have given. Keep the monthly report going, and hold one meeting a year to read the rules again. Change them together when the group changes.

titles.card_line: Set up a monthly money plan and a weekly spending check for your household.
titles.end_state: By week four you will have a written list of your income and fixed bills. You will also know where spending usually runs over. You will have a monthly plan and a quick weekly check that takes a few minutes. You will also have held one household money meeting and written down what you will change next month. It is a routine for the household, not a lecture about saving.
who_for: Households that run short before the month ends
Couples and families who share one budget
Anyone who has never written their spending down

letters.title: A welcome from Wanjiru Kamau-Otieno
letters.body: {first_name}, welcome. Nobody finds their first budget easy, and most of us avoid looking. This workbook starts gently. Write down what comes in, what goes out and where it usually runs over.

letters.title: A note for week 2
letters.body: {first_name}, the plan is made. Now a short weekly check. Five minutes with your list is enough. If a week goes over, write down why and move on to the next.

letters.title: A note for week 3
letters.body: {first_name}, this week you hold a household money meeting. Keep it short and kind. Everyone gets a turn to say what matters to them. Write down one change and agree a date.

letters.title: A note for week 4
letters.body: {first_name}, thank you for finishing. Keep the weekly check going. Next month, start a fresh page and carry forward what worked.

titles.card_line: Find an amount you can save each month and keep it going in a tight month.
titles.end_state: You will have chosen a realistic monthly amount and a safe place to keep it. You will have set the saving to happen on its own, with a name for what it is for. You will also have a short plan for a tight month, so one hard month trims the habit rather than ending it. The workbook gives no figures to chase. The amount is yours, and it can start small.
who_for: People who mean to save and never quite start
Households with an irregular income
Anyone whose saving stops after one hard month

letters.title: A welcome from Wanjiru Kamau-Otieno
letters.body: {first_name}, welcome. A saving habit does not start with a big sum. It starts with an amount you will not miss. This workbook helps you find yours and a safe place to keep it.

letters.title: A note for week 2
letters.body: {first_name}, set the habit up so it happens without your effort. Give the saving a name. A pot called new roof is kept more readily than one called savings.

letters.title: A note for week 4
letters.body: {first_name}, a tight month will arrive. This week you write the plan for it. Decide in advance how low the amount can go before it stops, and when it restarts.

letters.title: A note for week 6
letters.body: {first_name}, thank you for the six weeks. Look at what you have put aside, however small. Keep the habit going and raise the amount only when it feels comfortable.

titles.card_line: Start a weekly shared meal and a family question jar.
titles.end_state: Over eight weeks you will have a weekly shared meal that the family looks forward to, and a question jar that gets used. You will have a fair way to share chores as a contribution to the household. You will also have a simple routine for repairing after an argument, and a short page of family values written together. The page goes on the fridge and gets read again each season.
who_for: Parents who want family values to show up in daily life
Households with busy evenings and few shared meals
Families who want a fair way to share chores

letters.title: A welcome from Thandiwe Mokoena-Dube
letters.body: {first_name}, welcome. In our house the dinner table did most of the teaching. This workbook is about small routines, not grand plans. Choose one meal a week and make it yours.

letters.title: A note for week 2
letters.body: {first_name}, chores are next. Talk about them as a way of contributing, not a punishment. Let the children choose some jobs. People look after what they helped to decide.

letters.title: A note for week 4
letters.body: {first_name}, arguments happen in every family. What matters is how you mend things afterwards. Try a calm word and a simple apology the same evening, or the next morning.

letters.title: A note for week 6
letters.body: {first_name}, you are writing the family values together. Keep the list short. Three or four lines everyone can say aloud are enough. Pin it somewhere you all see it.

letters.title: A note for week 8
letters.body: {first_name}, thank you for the work you have done. Read the page again in a season. Change a line when the family has changed. The routines will carry on without much effort.

titles.card_line: Agree a family screen plan, an evening wind-down and one slower day a week.
titles.end_state: You will have noticed your family's current routines without blame, and written them down. You will then have a screen plan the whole family has agreed, and an evening wind-down that fits your house. You will also have a slower day each week and a short review done together. The plans are written in the family's own words and kept where everyone can see them.
who_for: Parents who feel screens take over the evening
Families who want calmer bedtimes
Households that want one slower day a week

letters.title: A welcome from Thandiwe Mokoena-Dube
letters.body: {first_name}, welcome. Please set blame aside for the first two weeks. Notice what happens in your house on an ordinary day. That is all this workbook asks to begin with.

letters.title: A note for week 2
letters.body: {first_name}, you have a picture of the current routines. Now draw up a screen plan together. Let the children say what they want too. A plan they helped write is far easier to keep.

letters.title: A note for week 4
letters.body: {first_name}, the evening wind-down is next. Keep it short and the same each night. Lower lights, a warm drink and a few quiet minutes. Adjust until it suits you.

letters.title: A note for week 6
letters.body: {first_name}, thank you for finishing. Hold a family review and ask each person what to keep. Keep the slower day, even when the week is busy.

titles.card_line: Choose three priorities each day and finish the day with a clean shutdown.
titles.end_state: You will have emptied your head into a single list and learned to pick three priorities from it. You will have a weekly planning slot, a polite way to say no, and a short end-of-day shutdown that closes the work. A monthly review ties it together. By week six the to-do list is shorter, and every item on it is one you chose. The method fits in a notebook.
who_for: People whose to-do list never gets shorter
Project leads who say yes too often
Anyone who carries work worries into the evening

letters.title: A welcome from Meenakshi Iyer-Rao
letters.body: {first_name}, welcome. For fifteen years I kept long lists and felt behind on all of them. This workbook is about doing fewer things with more care. Begin by emptying your head onto paper.

letters.title: A note for week 2
letters.body: {first_name}, weekly planning is the heart of this method. Give it forty minutes at the same time each week. Saying no politely comes next, and it takes time.

letters.title: A note for week 4
letters.body: {first_name}, you now close each day with a shutdown. Write tomorrow's three things and say aloud that the day is done. It sounds small. It makes a real difference to the evening.

letters.title: A note for week 6
letters.body: {first_name}, thank you for the six weeks. Hold your monthly review and cut anything that no longer earns its place. A shorter list is a good sign.

titles.card_line: Protect one morning block for your best work and keep it when the week gets busy.
titles.end_state: By week four you will know when you think best and what interrupts you then. You will have a protected morning block in your diary and a short start ritual that gets you into the work. You will also have a plan for keeping the block when a busy week arrives. The result is one reliable stretch of focused time that colleagues know about and respect.
who_for: People whose best hours go to email and messages
Anyone with demanding work that needs a clear head
Teams who want a shared quiet time

letters.title: A welcome from Meenakshi Iyer-Rao
letters.body: {first_name}, welcome. Most of us give our best hours to whatever arrives first. This workbook asks you to give them to the work that matters instead. Start by finding out when you think best.

letters.title: A note for week 2
letters.body: {first_name}, set the block in your diary and tell people about it. A small start ritual helps. Make a drink, close your messages and write one line about what you will finish.

letters.title: A note for week 3
letters.body: {first_name}, the first busy week will test the block. Decide now what counts as a real emergency. Everything else can wait until the block has ended.

letters.title: A note for week 4
letters.body: {first_name}, thank you for finishing. Look at the work you completed in your mornings. Keep the block, and protect it as you would any other appointment.

titles.card_line: Run meetings from a postcard agenda that ends with a decision.
titles.end_state: You will have looked honestly at a week of meetings and listed their purpose. You will have a postcard agenda format, a timebox for each item and a short decision note that goes out afterwards. You will also have cancelled, merged or replaced the meetings that were not earning their place. In four weeks the diary is lighter, and the meetings you keep end with something decided.
who_for: People who spend most of their week in meetings
Team leads who run recurring meetings
Anyone who leaves meetings unsure what was decided

letters.title: A welcome from Meenakshi Iyer-Rao
letters.body: {first_name}, welcome. Count the hours you spent in meetings last week, and write down what each one was for. The answer is often a surprise. This workbook begins with that honest count.

letters.title: A note for week 2
letters.body: {first_name}, try the postcard agenda. It has four lines: the purpose, the question, the time and the decision needed. If an item will not fit on the card, it is not ready.

letters.title: A note for week 3
letters.body: {first_name}, cancelling meetings takes courage. Start with one that has no clear purpose. Tell people what will replace it. Most are relieved.

letters.title: A note for week 4
letters.body: {first_name}, thank you for finishing. Keep the decision notes going. After a month, check again which meetings the notes show were worth holding.

titles.card_line: Say a hard thing kindly, listen back, and repair afterwards.
titles.end_state: By the end you will have written out what you want to say to someone you love and what you hope to keep. You will have practised an opening line, listening back and staying with the conversation when it gets hard. You will also have a plan for repairing afterwards and a clear sense of when to step away. These live in a notebook you can return to before the next difficult talk.
who_for: People preparing for a hard conversation with someone close
Anyone who avoids saying difficult things
Couples, friends and relatives who keep missing each other

letters.title: A welcome from Clodagh Ní Fhaoláin-Burke
letters.body: {first_name}, welcome. After years of sitting at kitchen tables with people in the middle of an argument, I have learned that preparation matters. This workbook begins with what you want to say and what you hope to keep.

letters.title: A note for week 2
letters.body: {first_name}, you are practising opening lines now. Keep them short and kind. Say what you have noticed and how it affects you. Then stop and let the other person answer.

letters.title: A note for week 4
letters.body: {first_name}, listening back is the hardest skill. Repeat what you heard before you reply. It slows everything down in the best way. Practise on something small first.

letters.title: A note for week 6
letters.body: {first_name}, thank you for working through this. Not every conversation goes well. Repair is part of the skill, and so is knowing when to step away and return another day.

titles.card_line: Build a weekly check-in and a shared plan for the year ahead as a couple.
titles.end_state: You will have a weekly check-in that you both keep, and a running note of what went well between you. You will have talked through the old stories that come up and written down how you want to disagree fairly. By week eight you will have a shared plan for the year ahead, in your own words, on a page you can both read. The notebook stays with the two of you.
who_for: Couples who want a regular, unhurried talk
Partners whose weeks pass without a proper conversation
Anyone who wants a plan they build together

letters.title: A welcome from Clodagh Ní Fhaoláin-Burke
letters.body: {first_name}, welcome. Long marriages are held together by small things done often. This workbook asks for one check-in a week and a habit of noticing what goes well. Begin there, together.

letters.title: A note for week 2
letters.body: {first_name}, old stories surface in every household. The aim now is not to win them. Write down what each of you remembers and listen to the other version without correcting it.

letters.title: A note for week 4
letters.body: {first_name}, disagreements are part of any partnership. This week you agree how to have them fairly. Choose a signal for a pause, and a time to return to the subject.

letters.title: A note for week 6
letters.body: {first_name}, thank you for the care you have put in. Look at the plan you have written for the year ahead. Pin a copy where you can both see it, and read it again in the spring.

letters.title: A note for week 8
letters.body: {first_name}, this is the last week. Keep the weekly check-in going. It is the part of this workbook that matters most.

titles.card_line: Turn what you have done into a plan for a new line of work.
titles.end_state: You will have a written account of what you have done, what you enjoyed and what you can carry into a new line of work. You will have run some small tests, held a few conversations and looked at a short course. By week eight you will have a money plan for the move and a first application drafted. The notebook gives you a clear next step, whether that is to go ahead or to wait.
who_for: People in mid-career thinking about a different line of work
Anyone laid off or bored and unsure what comes next
Those who want to test a change before leaving a job

letters.title: A welcome from Hester Quarrington
letters.body: {first_name}, welcome. My own change of direction came at forty-one, after twenty years in retail. It was frightening and it was possible. This workbook helps you take stock before you leap. Start by writing down what you have done.

letters.title: A note for week 2
letters.body: {first_name}, now you test the ideas. Keep the tests small: a conversation, an afternoon of shadowing, a short online lesson. Each one tells you something real.

letters.title: A note for week 4
letters.body: {first_name}, the money question has to be faced at some point. This week you write down what a change would cost and how long you could manage. Honest figures are kinder than hopeful ones.

letters.title: A note for week 6
letters.body: {first_name}, thank you for the time you have given. Whatever you decide, you now know your own skills better. Draft that first application, even if you wait before sending it.

letters.title: A note for week 8
letters.body: {first_name}, you are at the end of the eight weeks. Keep the notebook close and update it as things change.

titles.card_line: Prepare and rehearse what you will say when you ask about your pay.
titles.end_state: By the end you will have a short file of your results and what comparable roles pay, collected before the meeting. You will have written out what you want to say and rehearsed it aloud until it sounds like you. You will also have a plan for the meeting itself, for the reply you might hear and for the follow-up email afterwards. It gives you a clear script. The outcome is not promised.
who_for: Employees preparing to ask for a pay review
Anyone who dreads talking about money at work
People who want to raise the subject calmly and be heard

letters.title: A welcome from Hester Quarrington
letters.body: {first_name}, welcome. Asking about pay is uncomfortable for most of us, including me. Preparation makes it easier. This workbook starts with facts: your results and what comparable roles pay.

letters.title: A note for week 2
letters.body: {first_name}, write out what you want to say, then say it aloud. Doing so feels odd and works well. Keep it short, and say the figure you have in mind clearly.

letters.title: A note for week 3
letters.body: {first_name}, rehearse with a friend this week if you can. Ask them to reply in the ways you fear most. Practise a calm answer to each one.

letters.title: A note for week 4
letters.body: {first_name}, the meeting is here. Listen to the whole reply before you respond. Send your follow-up email the same day. Thank you for the care you have taken.

titles.card_line: Choose five stories from your working life and practise telling them aloud.
titles.end_state: You will have chosen five moments from your working life and shaped each one into a short story with a clear beginning, middle and end. You will have matched each story to the questions interviewers tend to ask. By the last week you will have said your answers aloud, more than once, and written a short note on what you would change. Five stories cover most of what an interview asks.
who_for: People with an interview coming up
Anyone who goes blank when asked about their experience
Career changers who need to explain what they bring

letters.title: A welcome from Hester Quarrington
letters.body: {first_name}, welcome. Interviews feel like an exam, but they are really a conversation about your work. This workbook asks you to choose five moments from your career that you are proud of, or that taught you something.

letters.title: A note for week 2
letters.body: {first_name}, shape each story now. Give it a beginning, a middle and an end. Keep to about two minutes. Say what you did, not only what the team did.

letters.title: A note for week 3
letters.body: {first_name}, match the stories to likely questions. One story can answer several. Make a short list and keep it by you when you rehearse.

letters.title: A note for week 4
letters.body: {first_name}, say the answers out loud this week. Record yourself if you can bear to. Thank you for the work you have done. The rest is rehearsal, and you are ready.

titles.card_line: Give feedback in short everyday conversations and ask for it in return.
titles.end_state: By week six you will have a habit of noticing what to praise and what to raise, written down as you see it. You will have held short feedback conversations and followed up on each one. You will also have asked your own team for feedback on how you manage, and written down what you heard. These conversations are brief, specific and regular, and they happen over coffee, not in a formal review.
who_for: Managers who save feedback for the annual review
Team leads who find praise or criticism awkward
Anyone who wants to hear how they come across

letters.title: A welcome from Marcus Delacroix-Hayes
letters.body: {first_name}, welcome. In restaurant kitchens, feedback has to be quick or it is useless. This workbook borrows that habit. Begin by noticing, each day, one thing worth praising and one worth raising.

letters.title: A note for week 2
letters.body: {first_name}, the short conversations start now. Pick a specific moment, say what you saw and ask what they think. Keep it under five minutes. Follow up a week later.

letters.title: A note for week 4
letters.body: {first_name}, this is the week to ask for feedback on your own work. It is the hardest step. Ask one question and listen to the answer without defending yourself.

letters.title: A note for week 6
letters.body: {first_name}, thank you for finishing. Feedback is a habit, not an event. Keep a notebook of the conversations you have had and review it once a month.

titles.card_line: Keep a decision log and explain your choices so people can follow them.
titles.end_state: You will have a simple decision log and a habit of deciding who to consult before a choice is made. You will have explained a number of your decisions in plain words, heard the objections and noted them. You will also have looked back at past decisions without blame, and written down what you would do the same way again. It all lives in one log that your team can read.
who_for: Team leads who make decisions their team cannot follow
Managers who want fewer surprises and less second-guessing
Anyone who wants a clearer record of why things were decided

letters.title: A welcome from Marcus Delacroix-Hayes
letters.body: {first_name}, welcome. People rarely mind a decision they understand. They mind one that arrives without a reason. This workbook begins with a decision log. Write down the choice, who you asked and why.

letters.title: A note for week 2
letters.body: {first_name}, explaining decisions takes courage. Say what you chose, what you gave up and why. Then listen to the objections. Write them down, even the ones you disagree with.

letters.title: A note for week 4
letters.body: {first_name}, this week you look back. Pick three old decisions and ask what you knew at the time. Do it without blame. The aim is to learn, not to judge anyone.

letters.title: A note for week 6
letters.body: {first_name}, thank you for the work. Keep the log open on your desk. A decision written down is easier to explain and easier to revisit.

titles.card_line: Define a role, hire fairly and plan the first month for a new team member.
titles.end_state: You will have a written description of each role you are hiring for, including what it is not. You will have fair interview questions, a plan for references and a clear offer. For every new person you will also have a first-month plan with early check-ins. By week six you have the first steps for hiring one person well. You can use them again for the next one.
who_for: Owners and managers about to hire for the first time
Small businesses growing from one person to a few
Anyone who wants hiring to feel fair and orderly

letters.title: A welcome from Marcus Delacroix-Hayes
letters.body: {first_name}, welcome. My first hires were made in a hurry, and I paid for it. This workbook slows you down in the right places. Start by writing what the role is, and what it is not.

letters.title: A note for week 2
letters.body: {first_name}, interviews and offers come next. Ask each person the same questions and write down their answers. It is fairer for them and gives you something to compare.

letters.title: A note for week 4
letters.body: {first_name}, a good first month does more than a good interview. Plan it now. Write down who they will meet, what they will learn and when you will check in.

letters.title: A note for week 6
letters.body: {first_name}, thank you for finishing. Hiring is a skill, and you now have notes to build on. Keep them, and update them after each new hire.

titles.card_line: Move into your first flat with a lease understood and your bills in order.
titles.end_state: You will have read your lease and understood it, with questions written down for the landlord or agent. You will have a list for your first week, a plan for paying bills and a monthly check. By week six you will also have a fair system for cleaning, shopping and sharing jobs with housemates. It all sits on a few pages that you can keep with your documents.
who_for: Young people moving out for the first time
Anyone setting up a home on their own
Housemates who want fair ways to share jobs and costs

letters.title: A welcome from Matilda Kershaw-Nguyen
letters.body: {first_name}, welcome. My work is with young people setting up their first homes, and the same worries come up each time. This workbook takes them one at a time. Start with your lease.

letters.title: A note for week 2
letters.body: {first_name}, bills are next. Set up what you can to be paid on its own, and keep a monthly check in your calendar. Ten minutes once a month is enough.

letters.title: A note for week 4
letters.body: {first_name}, living with others takes a little agreement. Talk about cleaning, shopping and quiet hours early. Write the plan down and put it on the fridge.

letters.title: A note for week 6
letters.body: {first_name}, thank you for working through this. A first flat is a big step. Keep your pages together in one folder, and add to them as things change.

titles.card_line: Stock a basic cupboard and cook five meals for yourself.
titles.end_state: You will have a basic cupboard and a list of five meals you already like and can cook. You will know how to do one weekly shop and cook once for two nights. By week four you will be using leftovers well and will have added one new dish to your list. The whole plan is built for one person on an ordinary budget, with no special kit.
who_for: People cooking for themselves for the first time
Anyone tired of eating the same takeaway
Those who want a simple weekly shop and a few reliable meals

letters.title: A welcome from Matilda Kershaw-Nguyen
letters.body: {first_name}, welcome. Cooking for one can feel like too much effort for too little reward. This workbook keeps it small. Start by stocking a basic cupboard and writing down five meals you already like.

letters.title: A note for week 2
letters.body: {first_name}, this week you do one shop and cook once for two nights. Cook a little more than you need and keep the rest. It makes the second evening easy.

letters.title: A note for week 3
letters.body: {first_name}, leftovers can be dull or good. Try turning them into something new: a soup, a wrap, a fried rice. Add one new dish to your list.

letters.title: A note for week 4
letters.body: {first_name}, thank you for finishing. Keep the list of meals on the fridge, and add to it when something works. Supper for one can be a pleasure.

titles.card_line: Know where your stopcock is and fix the small jobs yourself.
titles.end_state: You will know where your stopcock and fuse box are, and have a basic toolkit of the right things. You will have fixed a dripping tap, cleared a blocked sink and tightened a loose fitting, one step at a time. You will also have a clear list of jobs never to attempt yourself. A way to brief a tradesperson means the job is done properly. It is written for ordinary homes and tenants.
who_for: Renters and new owners who rely on others for every small job
Anyone who wants a basic toolkit and the confidence to use it
People who want to brief a tradesperson properly

letters.title: A welcome from Matilda Kershaw-Nguyen
letters.body: {first_name}, welcome. Most small repairs are easier than they look. Some are not, and this workbook says which. Begin by finding your stopcock and fuse box before you ever need them.

letters.title: A note for week 2
letters.body: {first_name}, you tackle the small jobs now. Read each step before you start. Take your time, and keep a bucket and a towel to hand.

letters.title: A note for week 3
letters.body: {first_name}, a drip is easy. A leak behind a wall is not. This week you learn where to stop and when to call someone. There is no shame in that.

letters.title: A note for week 4
letters.body: {first_name}, thank you for finishing. Keep your toolkit in one place and your notes with it. Next time something breaks, you will know where to begin.

titles.card_line: Plan your revision week by week and arrive at the exam with a plan for the day.
titles.end_state: You will have topic maps for every subject, a revision calendar and a starting check of what you already know. You will have practised spaced revision, worked through past papers and fixed your weak spots one at a time. By the last week you will have sat timed papers, planned your rest days and written an exam-day plan. The plan is built for a real week with other things in it.
who_for: Students facing exams who do not know where to start
Anyone who revises in a rush and loses track
Parents and tutors who want a clear plan to share

letters.title: A welcome from Olivier Tremblay-Singh
letters.body: {first_name}, welcome. Revision feels easier when you can see the whole plan. This workbook builds it with you, one week at a time. Start by mapping what you need to know.

letters.title: A note for week 2
letters.body: {first_name}, a revision calendar only works if it fits your real week. Mark the hours you cannot use first, then fill the rest with short sessions. Leave gaps for the unexpected.

letters.title: A note for week 4
letters.body: {first_name}, past papers are the most useful thing you can do now. Do them in small pieces first, then in full. Mark them honestly and note what needs more time.

letters.title: A note for week 6
letters.body: {first_name}, timed papers can feel hard. That is normal this close to the exam. Keep your rest days. Rested minds recall better than tired ones.

letters.title: A note for week 8
letters.body: {first_name}, thank you for the work you have put in. Read your exam-day plan the night before. Pack your bag, set two alarms and go to bed on time.

titles.card_line: Take notes you can test yourself from before exams.
titles.end_state: You will have looked closely at how you take notes now and found what to change. You will have tried question-style notes and a weekly summary, and decided which suits your courses. By week four you will use your notes to quiz yourself before an exam, with a system that fits your subjects. Everything is built on paper or screen as you prefer, and nothing needs special software.
who_for: Students whose notes pile up and never get read
Anyone starting college or university
Learners who want to use their notes to test themselves

letters.title: A welcome from Olivier Tremblay-Singh
letters.body: {first_name}, welcome. Most students take notes the way they always have, without asking if it works. This workbook starts by looking at yours. Bring a few pages from a recent class.

letters.title: A note for week 2
letters.body: {first_name}, try question-style notes this week. Write a question in the margin for each key point. Later you cover the notes and answer the questions.

letters.title: A note for week 3
letters.body: {first_name}, a short weekly summary keeps the course in one piece. Write half a page on Fridays and leave it at that. It pays off at exam time.

letters.title: A note for week 4
letters.body: {first_name}, thank you for finishing. Before your next exam, use the notes to test yourself. Cover, recall, check. The method is simple and it builds well over time.

titles.card_line: Plan study time around your life and write your first essay.
titles.end_state: You will have written down why you are going back to study and found the hours in your week that you can use. You will have practised reading an academic text and written your first essay. By week six you will know who to ask for help and what to do in a busy week. The plan fits around work and family, and it can change as your life does.
who_for: Adults returning to study after years away
Parents and workers fitting study around a full life
Anyone nervous about essays and reading lists

letters.title: A welcome from Olivier Tremblay-Singh
letters.body: {first_name}, welcome. Many adults come to study with doubts. In my work as an adviser, I have seen that returning students are often the most committed. Begin by writing why you are going back.

letters.title: A note for week 2
letters.body: {first_name}, academic texts are written for experts. You do not have to read every word. This week you learn to skim, question and take notes. Then your first essay.

letters.title: A note for week 4
letters.body: {first_name}, asking for help is part of studying, not a sign that something is wrong. Find out who your adviser is and write down what you will ask.

letters.title: A note for week 6
letters.body: {first_name}, thank you for finishing. Busy weeks will come. Decide now what the smallest useful amount of study is, and keep to that when life crowds in.

titles.card_line: Write three small rules for your days and learn how to restart them after a gap.
titles.end_state: You will have noticed the days that already go well and written down what they have in common. You will have written three small rules for ordinary days and tested each one. By week six you will know how to restart after a gap without fuss, and you will have revised your rules to fit. The notebook holds your own rules, in your own words, and nothing is counted or scored.
who_for: People who start habits and drop them
Anyone who wants rules that bend rather than break
Readers who like a small notebook and a simple plan

letters.title: A welcome from Friederike Ostwald-Rehm
letters.body: {first_name}, welcome. My notebook of small rules for living holds nothing clever. They are only easy to start and easy to restart. Over two weeks, you notice what already works for you.

letters.title: A note for week 2
letters.body: {first_name}, write three rules now. Keep them small enough to do on a tired day. Test each for a week and keep only those that earn their place.

letters.title: A note for week 4
letters.body: {first_name}, a gap does not break the rules. It is part of living. This week you practise restarting, without a fuss and without a lecture.

letters.title: A note for week 6
letters.body: {first_name}, thank you for the six weeks. Revise your rules when your life changes. The notebook is yours to rewrite as often as you like.

titles.card_line: Set up a short weekly reset for your home and your diary.
titles.end_state: You will have written down what clutters your week, in your space and in your diary, and chosen what to clear first. You will have a weekly reset routine for both, short enough to keep in a busy week. By week four you will have adjusted it to fit your life. The routine is a few lines on a card and takes around half an hour. It is not a deep clean.
who_for: People whose home and diary both feel crowded
Anyone who wants a short routine rather than a big tidy
Households that want a weekly reset

letters.title: A welcome from Friederike Ostwald-Rehm
letters.body: {first_name}, welcome. Designing buildings has taught me that most clutter is a decision not yet made. Start with a short list of what clutters your week and what you would clear first.

letters.title: A note for week 2
letters.body: {first_name}, a weekly reset has a few parts: clear surfaces, check the diary and plan the days ahead. Write yours on a card. Keep it short enough to do on a Sunday evening.

letters.title: A note for week 3
letters.body: {first_name}, you now have a routine. Try it for two weeks. If a step feels like a chore, cut it. A reset should leave you with more room.

letters.title: A note for week 4
letters.body: {first_name}, thank you for finishing. Keep the card where you will see it. Adjust it when your week changes, and do not hold yourself to anyone else's rules.

titles.card_line: Make a short list of friends who matter and reach out to each one.
titles.end_state: You will have a short, honest list of the people who matter to you and a note of when you last spoke. You will have reached out to several of them with a simple message or invitation, and set up a few regular plans. By week six you will also have tried to repair one lapsed friendship. The list is for you alone, and the plans are small enough to keep.
who_for: Adults whose friendships have drifted with work or moves
Anyone who always waits for others to get in touch
People who want to repair a friendship that lapsed

letters.title: A welcome from Rafael Moreira Lins
letters.body: {first_name}, welcome. Three moves in ten years taught me that friendships slip each time. This workbook is about keeping them going on purpose. Begin with a short list of who matters.

letters.title: A note for week 2
letters.body: {first_name}, reach out this week. A short message is enough: I was thinking of you, shall we meet? Most people are pleased to hear. Suggest a date.

letters.title: A note for week 4
letters.body: {first_name}, a lapsed friendship can be mended with an honest word. Say you have missed them and ask how they are. Do not argue about who stopped writing first.

letters.title: A note for week 6
letters.body: {first_name}, thank you for finishing. Keep your regular plans in the diary. Friendships are kept alive by showing up, and being a good guest as well as a good host.

titles.card_line: Find where people gather near you and join one regular thing.
titles.end_state: You will have a map of the places near you where people gather, from clubs to classes to cafes. You will have joined one regular activity and followed up with the people you met there. By week six you will also have hosted something small and kept in touch with old friends elsewhere. The workbook gives you a plan for the first months in a new town, one step at a time.
who_for: People who have just moved to a new town or city
Anyone starting again after a change of job or home
Readers who want to build a network of friends without forcing it

letters.title: A welcome from Rafael Moreira Lins
letters.body: {first_name}, welcome. Hello from Number Twelve is named for the first house where I knew nobody. Making friends in a new place takes patience. Begin by mapping where people gather near you.

letters.title: A note for week 2
letters.body: {first_name}, this week you join one regular thing. Choose a place that meets weekly, so you see the same faces. Follow up with a short message to someone you met.

letters.title: A note for week 4
letters.body: {first_name}, hosting something small can feel daunting. A cup of tea and a plate of biscuits is plenty. Invite two people and see what happens.

letters.title: A note for week 6
letters.body: {first_name}, thank you for finishing. Keep your old friends close as you make new ones. A call or a message each month keeps both going.

titles.card_line: Fit a ten-minute pause into your day and keep it on busy days.
titles.end_state: You will have found a time and a place for a daily pause. You will have tried it with tea, sound, a few breaths or a short walk. You will have chosen the form that fits you and written down how you will keep it when the day is crowded. By week four you have a ten-minute pause that belongs to you. The workbook asks for nothing else, and no pause is ever counted or scored.
who_for: People whose days run from one task to the next
Anyone who wants a small, regular break
Readers who prefer plain, practical suggestions

letters.title: A welcome from Haruka Tanabe-Ellis
letters.body: {first_name}, welcome. In the tea room, a pause is part of the work, not a reward for finishing it. This workbook asks for ten minutes a day. Begin by choosing a time and a place.

letters.title: A note for week 2
letters.body: {first_name}, try a few forms this week. Tea, a quiet sound, a short walk or a few slow breaths. Keep whichever feels most natural. Leave the others.

letters.title: A note for week 3
letters.body: {first_name}, a crowded day is when the pause is hardest to keep. Decide now how you will protect it. Even a shorter version still counts as yours.

letters.title: A note for week 4
letters.body: {first_name}, thank you for the four weeks. Keep your pause in whatever form suits you. If you miss a day, begin again the next. Nothing here is counted.

titles.card_line: Lower the lights, set a simple wind-down and plan for late nights and travel.
titles.end_state: You will have noticed how your evenings run now, without judging them. You will have set up a lower-light hour and a simple wind-down that suits your home. By week four you will have a short plan for late nights and for travel, so the routine bends when it needs to. These are small changes written in your own words. The workbook makes no promise about sleep.
who_for: People whose evenings are bright, busy and screen-heavy
Anyone who wants a gentler end to the day
Readers who like short, practical routines

letters.title: A welcome from Haruka Tanabe-Ellis
letters.body: {first_name}, welcome. In my house the evenings are quiet by habit, not by rule. This workbook asks you to notice your own evenings first, as they are. There is nothing to fix this week.

letters.title: A note for week 2
letters.body: {first_name}, this week you try a lower-light hour. Turn down the lamps and put screens aside if you can. Choose a simple wind-down of two or three steps.

letters.title: A note for week 3
letters.body: {first_name}, you are adjusting the routine now. Keep what suits you and drop what feels like an effort. A routine should fit your home, not the other way round.

letters.title: A note for week 4
letters.body: {first_name}, thank you for the four weeks. Late nights and travel will come. Write a shorter version of your evening for those times, and return to the full one when you can.

titles.card_line: Put real breaks into your week with tea, short walks and screen-free lunches.
titles.end_state: You will have looked at where your week has no breaks at all. You will have tried tea breaks, short walks and screen-free lunches, and kept the ones that suit you. By week four you will have asked the people around you to respect your breaks, and written down how. The result is a plan for a slower pace in a busy week. It is yours to adjust.
who_for: People whose weeks have no natural pauses
Anyone who eats at their desk
Readers who want to slow the pace in small ways

letters.title: A welcome from Haruka Tanabe-Ellis
letters.body: {first_name}, welcome. A busy week does not have to be a hurried one. This workbook is about small breaks put in on purpose. Begin by marking where your week has none.

letters.title: A note for week 2
letters.body: {first_name}, try a tea break, a short walk and a lunch without a screen. Keep the ones that feel natural. Do not add pressure. A break is not another task.

letters.title: A note for week 3
letters.body: {first_name}, other people matter too. This week you tell the people around you about your breaks. A plain sentence and a calm tone are enough.

letters.title: A note for week 4
letters.body: {first_name}, thank you for finishing. Keep the breaks that earned a place in your week. They can be small. What matters is that they stay.

titles.card_line: Pay yourself a steady monthly wage from uneven freelance income.
titles.end_state: You will have a year of income laid out at a glance and an honest figure for your real monthly costs. You will have a holding account, a monthly wage you pay yourself and a buffer that evens out the lean months. By week six you will also set aside money for tax and have a plan for quiet months. The workbook is about habits and records. It does not give tax advice.
who_for: Freelancers whose income arrives in lumps
Self-employed people who dread the quiet months
Anyone who wants a steady monthly wage from uneven pay

letters.title: A welcome from Ximena Ruiz-Albarrán
letters.body: {first_name}, welcome. After twenty years of freelancing, I know the feeling of a great month followed by an empty one. This workbook starts with the facts: a year of income on one page and your real monthly costs.

letters.title: A note for week 2
letters.body: {first_name}, you now have a holding account. Pay all your income into it and pay yourself a fixed wage once a month. It feels strange for the first few weeks. Keep going.

letters.title: A note for week 4
letters.body: {first_name}, tax is the next step. Set aside a portion of each payment as it arrives. Check the rules for your own situation with a qualified adviser. This workbook does not give tax advice.

letters.title: A note for week 6
letters.body: {first_name}, thank you for finishing. Plan for quiet months while the busy ones are still fresh. A buffer is just a promise to your future self.

titles.card_line: Send clear invoices, chase late ones with a script and hold a monthly money hour.
titles.end_state: You will know what you are owed and how long payment usually takes. You will have an invoice that is clear, payment terms you can state with confidence and a short script for chasing a late payment. By week four you will have a monthly money hour in your diary, where invoices and savings are looked at together. The method suits freelancers and small suppliers, and it is written in plain words.
who_for: Freelancers and small suppliers waiting on payments
Anyone uncomfortable chasing an invoice
People who want one regular hour for money

letters.title: A welcome from Ximena Ruiz-Albarrán
letters.body: {first_name}, welcome. Chasing payment is awkward for most of us. The trick is to prepare, so that asking feels like routine. Begin by listing what you are owed and how long it usually takes.

letters.title: A note for week 2
letters.body: {first_name}, this week you write the chasing script. Keep it polite and short. State the invoice number, the amount and the date it was due. Ask for a date by which it will be paid.

letters.title: A note for week 3
letters.body: {first_name}, clear invoices get paid sooner. Put the due date and the payment details at the top. Make it easy for the other person to say yes.

letters.title: A note for week 4
letters.body: {first_name}, thank you for finishing. Keep the monthly money hour in your calendar. One hour on invoices and savings is time well spent.

titles.card_line: Stay close to your teenager by listening more and agreeing house rules together.
titles.end_state: Over eight weeks you will have noticed when your teenager talks and practiced listening more. You will have agreed house rules together and worked out how to handle a row. By the end you will also have plans for more independence, regular check-ins and a way to build trust in both directions. It is written for ordinary households. It does not promise that your teenager will change.
who_for: Parents of teenagers who feel shut out
Anyone whose house rules cause daily arguments
Families that want more trust in both directions

letters.title: A welcome from Ligaya Abellera-Cruz
letters.body: {first_name}, welcome. As a guidance counselor and a mother, I have spent many evenings on the stairs, hoping for a word. This workbook is about listening more. Begin by noticing when your teenager talks.

letters.title: A note for week 2
letters.body: {first_name}, house rules work best when your teenager has a say. Sit down together and write them in plain words. Keep the list short and agree the consequences in advance.

letters.title: A note for week 4
letters.body: {first_name}, rows will happen. Aim to stay calm and return to the subject later. A short, honest apology from the adult often opens the door.

letters.title: A note for week 6
letters.body: {first_name}, independence comes in steps. Offer a little more, agree a check-in and see how it goes. Trust grows from small, kept agreements.

letters.title: A note for week 8
letters.body: {first_name}, thank you for the work you have put in. Keep the check-ins going. Teenagers grow up quickly, and these small habits will last.

titles.card_line: Set a time, a place and a short check-in for homework evenings.
titles.end_state: You will have watched how homework evenings go now, and written down what works and what does not. You will have set a regular time and place and agreed a short check-in with your child. By week six you will also know how to work with teachers and how to hand responsibility over, bit by bit. The plans are short, and your child helps to write them.
who_for: Parents who dread the homework hour
Families with arguments every school night
Caregivers who want to step back as children grow

letters.title: A welcome from Ligaya Abellera-Cruz
letters.body: {first_name}, welcome. Homework evenings can feel like a battle, and in my house they sometimes were. This workbook begins with watching, not fixing. Write down how the evenings go now.

letters.title: A note for week 2
letters.body: {first_name}, set a time and a place this week. Agree both with your child. Keep the check-in short: what is due, what is hard, what do you need from me?

letters.title: A note for week 4
letters.body: {first_name}, teachers want to help. A short note to explain what is happening at home usually gets a warm reply. Ask what they would like you to do.

letters.title: A note for week 6
letters.body: {first_name}, thank you for finishing. Handing over responsibility is gradual. Offer a little more each month, and let your child learn from small mistakes.

titles.card_line: Put both calendars on one page and hold a Sunday chat about the week.
titles.end_state: You will have both calendars on one page and a regular Sunday chat to go through the week ahead. You will have divided errands, lifts and appointments in a way you both agree is fair. By week six you will also have protected some time together and held a monthly review. The plan is simple enough to keep, and it is yours to change as the seasons change.
who_for: Couples whose diaries collide every week
Partners who share errands, lifts and appointments
Households that want a calmer start to the week

letters.title: A welcome from Sofia Hedlund-Ahl
letters.body: {first_name}, welcome. In my work with families I have seen how often the week goes wrong because two diaries never met. This workbook puts them on one page. Begin with a Sunday chat.

letters.title: A note for week 2
letters.body: {first_name}, dividing errands and lifts is the next step. Be fair, and be specific. Name the person, the day and the time. Vague plans lead to quiet resentment.

letters.title: A note for week 4
letters.body: {first_name}, time together needs protecting too. Put it in the diary first, before the rest fills up. Give it the weight of any other appointment.

letters.title: A note for week 6
letters.body: {first_name}, thank you for finishing. Hold the monthly review and change what is not working. A shared week is never finished, only adjusted.

titles.card_line: List every household job, seen and unseen, and agree who owns each one.
titles.end_state: You will have a full list of household jobs, including the ones nobody sees, such as remembering and planning. You will have agreed who owns what, from start to finish, so that one person is not always the one who thinks of it. By week four you will have reviewed the split together and adjusted it fairly. The list and the agreement stay on a single page that you both keep.
who_for: Partners who disagree about who does what at home
Anyone who carries the mental load of the household
Couples who want a fair split they can review

letters.title: A welcome from Sofia Hedlund-Ahl
letters.body: {first_name}, welcome. Much of the work at home is invisible: remembering, planning, noticing. This workbook asks you to list all of it, the visible and the unseen, before talking about who does what.

letters.title: A note for week 2
letters.body: {first_name}, ownership is the key idea. If a job is yours, it is yours from start to finish. That includes remembering it. Agree the list together, one job at a time.

letters.title: A note for week 3
letters.body: {first_name}, review the split in a calm moment, not in the middle of an argument. Ask each other what feels fair. Adjust the list, and do not keep score.

letters.title: A note for week 4
letters.body: {first_name}, thank you for finishing. Look at the list again in a season. Households change, and a fair split changes with them.

titles.card_line: Share the work in a volunteer team with clear roles and rotas.
titles.end_state: You will have a clear picture of who does what in your team now and who is carrying too much. You will have written roles, a rota and a handover note for each job. By week six you will also have a plan for recruiting more help and a way to thank people properly. Everything is written for volunteers, who give their time freely and deserve a clear, fair system.
who_for: Leaders of clubs, charities and community groups
Volunteers who feel they carry too much
Anyone who wants to recruit and keep helpers

letters.title: A welcome from Tama Rāwiri-Hughes
letters.body: {first_name}, welcome. After years of coaching clubs and leading volunteers, I know that the same few people carry most of the load. This workbook helps your team to share it. Start by listing who does what.

letters.title: A note for week 2
letters.body: {first_name}, clear roles come next. Write each one on a page: what it involves, how long it takes and who to ask. A rota and a handover note keep things moving when people are away.

letters.title: A note for week 4
letters.body: {first_name}, recruiting help is easier when the jobs are small and defined. Ask for one task at a time. Be specific about the time it will take.

letters.title: A note for week 6
letters.body: {first_name}, thank you for finishing. Thank your volunteers by name and say what they did. It costs nothing and it is remembered.

titles.card_line: Run a first mentoring relationship, from the opening meeting to a plan for next season.
titles.end_state: You will have held a first meeting and agreed what your mentee wants from the relationship. You will have a bank of good questions, a few stories to share and small tasks to set. By week four you will have reviewed progress together and planned the next season. The workbook is short and practical. It is written for people who are mentoring for the first time and want to do it well.
who_for: First-time mentors in a club, workplace or community
Anyone asked to guide a newcomer
People who want a clear shape for each meeting

letters.title: A welcome from Tama Rāwiri-Hughes
letters.body: {first_name}, welcome. Mentoring is mostly listening, and a little asking. Years of coaching taught me that. This workbook gives you a shape for your first meetings. Start by agreeing what your mentee wants.

letters.title: A note for week 2
letters.body: {first_name}, good questions matter more than good advice. Prepare three before each meeting. Share a story only when it is useful to them, and keep it short.

letters.title: A note for week 3
letters.body: {first_name}, small tasks give the relationship shape. Set one between meetings and ask how it went. Celebrate what worked and talk about what did not.

letters.title: A note for week 4
letters.body: {first_name}, thank you for finishing. Review the season together and decide what comes next. Whatever you choose, thank your mentee for their time.

titles.card_line: Notice your inner voice and write fairer replies to it after a mistake.
titles.end_state: You will have noticed your inner voice and the moments when it gets loud, using a short note each day. You will have written fairer replies and tried kinder words after a mistake. By week six you will have a plan for keeping that voice in a busy week. These are written exercises in your own notebook. The workbook is not therapy and does not promise a result.
who_for: People who are hard on themselves after a mistake
Anyone who wants to notice their own inner voice
Readers who like short written exercises

letters.title: A welcome from Nadia Farouk-Hassan
letters.body: {first_name}, welcome. As a teacher, I hear how pupils speak to themselves, and how often they speak harshly. This workbook starts with listening to your own voice. Notice when it is loud and what it says.

letters.title: A note for week 2
letters.body: {first_name}, you now write fairer replies. Imagine saying the words to a friend. If they would sound unkind, change them. Keep what feels true and fair.

letters.title: A note for week 4
letters.body: {first_name}, mistakes still happen. This week you try kinder words afterwards. Write one sentence you would say to a friend in your place, and read it back to yourself.

letters.title: A note for week 6
letters.body: {first_name}, thank you for working through this. Busy weeks make the voice louder. Keep your notebook near. Help now is always at the top of the screen.

titles.card_line: Sort the week into must, should and could, and say one honest no.
titles.end_state: You will have seen your whole week on one page. You will have sorted what you have taken on into must, should and could, and said one honest no to something that did not fit. By week four you will have built small pockets of rest into the week and written down how you will protect them. The result is a plan that fits the week you really have, in your own handwriting.
who_for: People whose week holds more than it can carry
Carers, parents and workers pulled in several directions
Anyone who finds it hard to say no

letters.title: A welcome from Nadia Farouk-Hassan
letters.body: {first_name}, welcome. A full week asks a lot of you, and I know how easy it is to say yes to everything. Begin by writing the whole week on one page.

letters.title: A note for week 2
letters.body: {first_name}, now sort it. Write each item under one of three headings: must, should, could. Be honest. Many items you expected under must belong under could.

letters.title: A note for week 3
letters.body: {first_name}, this week you say one honest no. Keep it short and kind. A plain reply is better than a long explanation.

letters.title: A note for week 4
letters.body: {first_name}, thank you for finishing. Look at the pockets of rest you have built. Keep them in the diary, and add another when you can.

titles.card_line: Keep a window seat notebook and write down small things you notice as the week goes on.
titles.end_state: You will have chosen a window, a time and a notebook, and used them for five minutes a day. You will have written about light and weather, sound, and the moment before you reach for your phone. You will have noticed people and movement without judging them, and taken the habit to a bus, a queue or a desk. The final week is a look back through the notebook to choose what to keep.
who_for: People who want a quiet daily habit of noticing
Anyone who sits at a window and watches the day pass
Readers who enjoy a small notebook

letters.title: A welcome from Haruka Tanabe-Ellis
letters.body: {first_name}, welcome. In my tea room, the window was the best seat. This workbook asks for five minutes a day. Choose a window, a time and a notebook, and begin.

letters.title: A note for week 2
letters.body: {first_name}, sound is next, and the pause before you reach for a phone. Notice it and write it down. You need do nothing more.

letters.title: A note for week 4
letters.body: {first_name}, people and movement come into view now. Notice them without judging. A person at a bus stop, a cat on a wall. Write what is there.

letters.title: A note for week 6
letters.body: {first_name}, thank you for the six weeks. Read the notebook from the start and choose what to keep. Nothing here was counted, and nothing was missed.

titles.card_line: Write down your evenings as they are, then slow the last hour one week at a time.
titles.end_state: You will have written down what your evenings look like now, before changing anything. Week by week you will have lowered the lights and the noise for the last hour. You will have found a place for the phone away from your pillow, and shaped a short wind-down you like. You will have a plan for late shifts, visitors and travel. The sixth week is for keeping the hour that suits you and letting the rest go.
who_for: People whose evenings run late and loud
Shift workers and anyone with an irregular day
Readers who want one small change each week

letters.title: A welcome from Harnoor Dhaliwal-Fournier
letters.body: {first_name}, welcome. After years of working nights in a bakery, I know how hard it is to slow down at the end of the day. This workbook asks for one change a week. In the first, there is no change at all.

letters.title: A note for week 2
letters.body: {first_name}, the phone needs a place that is not your pillow. Choose somewhere across the room and charge it there. It is a small step.

letters.title: A note for week 4
letters.body: {first_name}, late shifts, guests and travel will interrupt. This week you plan for them. A shorter version of your wind-down will do on those nights.

letters.title: A note for week 6
letters.body: {first_name}, thank you for the six weeks. Keep the hour that suits you and let the rest go. Nothing here was counted, and nothing is owed.

titles.card_line: Write down what happened as plain facts and ask what a fair friend would say.
titles.end_state: You will have noticed the words you use about yourself after a mistake and written what happened as plain facts, with no verdict. You will have asked what a fair friend would say about the same day. Over eight weeks you will tell apart standards that serve you from those that only punish. You will make one repair after a real mistake and then let it rest. The workbook ends with a fairer way of looking at yourself.
who_for: People who judge themselves harshly after a mistake
Anyone who finds it hard to hear praise
Readers who want to write things down plainly

letters.title: A welcome from Nadia Farouk-Hassan
letters.body: {first_name}, welcome. A draft can be changed, and a verdict cannot. That is the idea behind this workbook. Begin by noticing the words you use about yourself after a mistake.

letters.title: A note for week 2
letters.body: {first_name}, writing the facts is your task now. Keep to what happened and leave out the judgement. It looks different on the page than it does in your head.

letters.title: A note for week 4
letters.body: {first_name}, high standards can serve you or punish you. This week you look at which are which. Be honest and be gentle. You are not marking yourself.

letters.title: A note for week 6
letters.body: {first_name}, a repair is a single, honest step. Say sorry, put a thing right or ask a question. Then let it rest. Not every mistake needs a long conversation.

letters.title: A note for week 8
letters.body: {first_name}, thank you for the eight weeks. Take your notebook with you into busy weeks. If a week is hard, Help now is at the top of every screen.

titles.card_line: Put the month on one page, hand back one commitment and book a rest hour.
titles.end_state: You will have put the whole month on one page and found the gaps in it. You will have handed back or turned down one commitment, using words written in advance. You will also have booked a rest hour and kept it like any other appointment. By week four you will have noticed what kind of rest suited you and planned next month. The result is a diary with real room in it.
who_for: People with a crowded diary and no room for rest
Anyone who struggles to turn down a request
Readers who want a plain monthly plan

letters.title: A welcome from Harnoor Dhaliwal-Fournier
letters.body: {first_name}, welcome. For years my diary held other people's priorities and none of my own. Begin by putting the whole month on one page and finding the gaps.

letters.title: A note for week 2
letters.body: {first_name}, this week you hand back one commitment. Write the words first. A short, polite message is enough. You do not owe a long reason.

letters.title: A note for week 3
letters.body: {first_name}, book a rest hour and keep it. Give it the weight of a meeting with someone you respect. Write what you did in it.

letters.title: A note for week 4
letters.body: {first_name}, thank you for finishing. Look at which rest suited you and plan next month. Keep the page on one sheet, where you can see it.

titles.card_line: Take one very small step at a time, and write a short plan of what to keep.
titles.end_state: You will have a gentle way to use this workbook, and you will know where Help now is. Over twelve weeks you will have kept a short daily note in your own words and chosen one very small task each day. You will have spent a few minutes outside, kept simple routines, and reached out to someone you trust. The last week gives you a short plan of what to keep and who to call.
who_for: People having heavy days who want small, doable steps
Readers who want to work at their own pace
Anyone who wants a plan to share with their GP or someone close

letters.title: A welcome from Delphine Arceneaux-Lim
letters.body: {first_name}, welcome. Heavy days are hard, and this workbook asks for very little. Please use it gently, at your own pace. If you need help now, you are not alone. Help now has people you can talk to today.

letters.title: A note for week 3
letters.body: {first_name}, you are three weeks in. The very small task is the heart of this workbook. Choose it the night before and make it so small that it is easy to begin.

letters.title: A note for week 6
letters.body: {first_name}, midway through, it is worth pausing. Read back over your notes. Some days will have been better than others, and that is part of how this goes.

letters.title: A note for week 9
letters.body: {first_name}, week nine is for the days that go badly. Starting again on any day is allowed. There is no catching up and nothing owed.

letters.title: A note for week 12
letters.body: {first_name}, thank you for the twelve weeks. Write down what you want to keep and who you would call. If you need help now, Help now is at the top of every screen.

titles.card_line: Walk ten minutes at the same time each day and plan a week of movement.
titles.end_state: You will have noticed how much you move now, with no targets. You will have chosen a ten-minute walk at a regular time. You will have found the movement already hidden in your week, such as stairs and errands. Over eight weeks you will try gentle stretching, moving with someone else, indoor options for wet days, and one new kind of movement. The last week gives you a weekly plan that fits your body and your diary.
who_for: People who want to move more in an ordinary week
Anyone who prefers walking to the gym
Readers who like small steps without targets

letters.title: A welcome from Gwenllian Pryce-Adeyemi
letters.body: {first_name}, welcome. A postal round of twenty years taught me that small steps add up. This workbook sets no targets. Begin by noticing how much you move now.

letters.title: A note for week 2
letters.body: {first_name}, you are three weeks in. Look for the movement already in your week: the stairs, the errands, the bus stop a street early. Write it down.

letters.title: A note for week 4
letters.body: {first_name}, stretching at the start and end of the day is next. Keep it gentle. Stop if anything hurts, and speak to your doctor if you are unsure what suits you.

letters.title: A note for week 6
letters.body: {first_name}, wet days and dark mornings arrive for everyone. This week you plan for them. A few minutes indoors counts as movement.

letters.title: A note for week 8
letters.body: {first_name}, thank you for the eight weeks. Look at the weekly plan you have written. Keep it flexible, and change it when your week changes.

titles.card_line: Cook one pot on a Sunday and eat it three ways during the week.
titles.end_state: You will have cooked a soup or stew from what was already in your cupboard, and cooked once to eat it three ways. You will have learned to store, cool and reheat food safely. By week four you will have a short list of pots you like and a weekly cooking slot in your diary. The recipes are plain and low in cost, and they are written for the week ahead.
who_for: People who want to cook once and eat several times
Households on a tight food budget
Anyone who wants a few reliable pots

letters.title: A welcome from Niamh Corrigan-Oduya
letters.body: {first_name}, welcome. Cooking for a large family taught me the value of a good pot. This workbook starts with what you already have in the cupboard. Choose a soup or a stew and cook it once.

letters.title: A note for week 2
