letters.body: {first_name}, cook once and eat three ways this week. The same stew can become a pie filling, a pasta sauce or a soup. It saves time and money.

letters.title: A note for week 3
letters.body: {first_name}, food safety is simple when you know the steps. Cool food quickly, store it covered and reheat it until hot all the way through.

letters.title: A note for week 4
letters.body: {first_name}, thank you for finishing. Write your list of favourite pots and put it on the fridge. A weekly cooking slot keeps the habit going.

titles.card_line: Plan a week of everyday meals and keep the shopping list on the fridge.
titles.end_state: You will have written down what you ate last week without judgement, and used it to plan a week of everyday meals. You will have a shopping list on the fridge that you add to through the week. You will also have a short set of meals you can make without much thought. By week six you will have adjusted the plan to your budget and your household. The workbook asks for no diet and no targets.
who_for: Households that decide dinner at five o'clock each day
Anyone who wastes food or money at the shop
People who want a simple weekly meal plan

letters.title: A welcome from Niamh Corrigan-Oduya
letters.body: {first_name}, welcome. A plain plan for the week makes dinner easier. This workbook starts with a look at what you ate last week. There is no judgement here, only a list.

letters.title: A note for week 2
letters.body: {first_name}, plan the week's meals now. Choose six and leave one night free. Write the shopping list from the plan, not from hope.

letters.title: A note for week 4
letters.body: {first_name}, keep the list on the fridge and add to it as things run out. It saves a trip and stops you buying twice.

letters.title: A note for week 6
letters.body: {first_name}, thank you for finishing. Adjust the plan for your budget and your household. A simple routine you keep is better than an ambitious one you drop.

titles.card_line: Shape a weekly pattern for the first year after full-time work.
titles.end_state: You will have written down what you will miss about work and what you will not. You will have a simple weekly shape with fixed points. You will have a way to keep in touch with people you saw daily, and something useful you do for others each week. Over eight weeks you will also find a way of moving that you enjoy and one new thing to try. The last week gives you a plan for the rest of the first year.
who_for: People about to retire, or newly retired
Anyone whose days have lost their shape
Couples adjusting to being at home together

letters.title: A welcome from Desmond Kalantzis-Webb
letters.body: {first_name}, welcome. After thirty years driving buses, my first weeks of retirement felt oddly empty. This workbook starts with an honest list of what you will miss about work and what you will not.

letters.title: A note for week 2
letters.body: {first_name}, you have a weekly shape now. Fixed points matter: a walk on Tuesday, a call on Friday. Add a way to keep in touch with the people you used to see every day.

letters.title: A note for week 4
letters.body: {first_name}, something useful for others each week can be small. A neighbour's shopping, a shift at the library, a letter to a friend. Choose what suits you.

letters.title: A note for week 6
letters.body: {first_name}, sharing a home with someone who is now around more takes patience on both sides. Talk about space and time apart. Write down what you agree.

letters.title: A note for week 8
letters.body: {first_name}, thank you for the eight weeks. Write the plan for the rest of your first year, and leave room in it. The first year of retirement is long, and it should be your own.

titles.card_line: Build a weekly pattern of learning, moving and company at seventy.
titles.end_state: You will have described what a good week looks like for you at this age and chosen one subject you have always been curious about. Over twelve weeks you will build a daily walk or gentle movement. You will find a club or class nearby and go once. You will also set up memory habits such as lists and a weekly diary. By the end you will have a weekly pattern of learning, moving and company to keep.
who_for: People in later life who want to keep learning
Anyone looking for a gentle weekly routine
Readers who prefer plain words and a slow pace

letters.title: A welcome from Desmond Kalantzis-Webb
letters.body: {first_name}, welcome. A good week at seventy looks different for each of us. This workbook begins by asking what yours looks like. Write it down in your own words.

letters.title: A note for week 3
letters.body: {first_name}, you are three weeks in. A daily walk or gentle movement that suits your body is the base for the rest. Go at your own pace. Check with your doctor if you are unsure what suits you.

letters.title: A note for week 6
letters.body: {first_name}, a club, a class or a group nearby is the next step. Go once. You need not return if it is not for you. Trying it is the aim.

letters.title: A note for week 9
letters.body: {first_name}, low-energy days come to everyone. Decide now what still counts as a good day. A cup of tea and one page of a book may be enough.

letters.title: A note for week 12
letters.body: {first_name}, thank you for the twelve weeks. Write the weekly pattern you want to keep, with learning, movement and company in it. Put it where you will see it each morning.

titles.card_line: Write the one sentence that says what you think, and say it aloud.
titles.end_state: You will have noticed the moments when you hold back and what that costs you. You will have written one sentence that says what you think or need, practised it aloud, and spoken up in a meeting or a queue. You will also have a way to handle pushback without over-explaining. By week six you will have reviewed what changed and chosen the next place to speak up. You stay yourself throughout.
who_for: Quiet people who want to be heard
Anyone who goes silent in meetings
Readers who dislike being pushed to become someone else

letters.title: A welcome from Mireille Okafor-Gauthier
letters.body: {first_name}, welcome. Twenty years on a library help desk taught me that quiet people have a great deal to say. This workbook does not ask you to become louder. It asks you to be clear. Begin by noticing when you hold back.

letters.title: A note for week 2
letters.body: {first_name}, now you write one sentence. Keep it plain: what you think, or what you need. Read it aloud to yourself until it sounds like you.

letters.title: A note for week 4
letters.body: {first_name}, speak up once this week, in a meeting or a queue. Say your sentence and then leave a pause. The pause is part of the sentence.

letters.title: A note for week 6
letters.body: {first_name}, thank you for the six weeks. Look at where you spoke up and what followed. Choose the next place, and write the sentence for it.

titles.card_line: Say no to small requests with three short sentences you have practised.
titles.end_state: You will have made a list of recent yeses you wish had been noes. You will have three short ways to say no and a sense of when to use each. You will have said no to one small request and noticed what followed. By week four you will have protected the time you freed and planned the next limit. Nothing here asks for a speech, and every line fits on a card.
who_for: People who say yes and regret it
Anyone who over-explains a refusal
Readers who want short, ready-made words

letters.title: A welcome from Mireille Okafor-Gauthier
letters.body: {first_name}, welcome. Many people find it hard to refuse a request. This workbook gives you short, kind sentences to use, and no speeches. Start by listing the recent yeses you wish had been noes.

letters.title: A note for week 2
letters.body: {first_name}, you now have three ways to say no. Practise them aloud. Try one on a small request this week, and notice what follows. The world usually carries on as before.

letters.title: A note for week 3
letters.body: {first_name}, protect the time you freed. Put something in the diary for it before someone else claims it.

letters.title: A note for week 4
letters.body: {first_name}, thank you for finishing. Plan the next limit and write the words for it. A polite no is a skill, and it gets easier each time.

titles.card_line: Work a big decision through on paper, from the options to a review date.
titles.end_state: You will have named the decision in one sentence, with the date you need to make it. You will have listed every option, including doing nothing, and written five plain words for what matters most. You will have compared the options in a simple table, asked the people affected and run a small test. By week eight you will have made the decision, written down why, and set a review date.
who_for: People facing a big choice and going round in circles
Anyone who wants to decide on paper, not in their head
Households making a joint decision

letters.title: A welcome from Bronwyn Achterberg-Lui
letters.body: {first_name}, welcome. In the hardware shop, the big decisions were made at the kitchen table, on paper. This workbook uses the same method. Start by naming the decision in one sentence, with a date.

letters.title: A note for week 2
letters.body: {first_name}, what matters most to you? Write it as five plain words. They become the columns of your table. Keep them honest, and do not borrow anyone else's.

letters.title: A note for week 4
letters.body: {first_name}, this week you ask the people affected. Listen to what they say and write it down. You do not have to agree with all of it.

letters.title: A note for week 6
letters.body: {first_name}, a small test before the full commitment is worth the time. Try a day, a trial run or a conversation. Note what you learn.

letters.title: A note for week 8
letters.body: {first_name}, thank you for the eight weeks. Set a review date and write what would make you change course. A decision can be revisited without shame.

titles.card_line: Pick three goals for the fridge and check them once a month.
titles.end_state: You will have chosen three goals from a longer wish list and written a first step for each, small enough for this week. You will have a five-minute weekly look at the list on your fridge. By week four you will have run a monthly check that lets you change a goal without guilt. The whole system is a single sheet of paper, three goals long, and it is easy to restart.
who_for: People with a long wish list and no plan
Anyone who drops goals after a few weeks
Readers who like one sheet of paper

letters.title: A welcome from Bronwyn Achterberg-Lui
letters.body: {first_name}, welcome. A long wish list is a burden. This workbook asks you to pick three goals. Start by writing the longer list, then choosing the three that matter most.

letters.title: A note for week 2
letters.body: {first_name}, write one first step for each goal. Make it small enough to do this week. A step you can do beats a plan you admire.

letters.title: A note for week 3
letters.body: {first_name}, look at the fridge list for five minutes each week. That is all. Move a step forward or write a new one.

letters.title: A note for week 4
letters.body: {first_name}, thank you for finishing. At the monthly check, change a goal if it no longer fits. That is good sense, and nothing to feel guilty about.

titles.card_line: Write letters to the next ten years and decide on one change to start this year.
titles.end_state: You will have written a letter about the life you have now, the good parts first. Over eight weeks you will write about what you want to keep and the people you want close. You will write about the work you want to be doing and what you are willing to let go. You will pick one change to start this year, with a first step. At the end you read the letters back and seal one for later.
who_for: People in midlife taking stock
Anyone who wants to write down what matters
Readers who like letters and a notebook

letters.title: A welcome from Theodora Valdez-Brennan
letters.body: {first_name}, welcome. After twenty-two years of driving a school bus, I began writing, and midlife looked different afterwards. This workbook starts with a letter about the life you have now. Put the good parts first.

letters.title: A note for week 2
letters.body: {first_name}, you have written about what you want to keep. Now the people you want close. Name them. Think about what time with each of them would look like.

letters.title: A note for week 4
letters.body: {first_name}, letting go is part of this. Write down what you are willing to release. It might be a habit, a role or a grudge.

letters.title: A note for week 6
letters.body: {first_name}, choose one change to start this year. Write the first step and the date. Keep it small enough to begin on a Monday.

letters.title: A note for week 8
letters.body: {first_name}, thank you for the eight weeks. Read the letters back and seal one for later. Put a date on the envelope. Open it when the date arrives.

titles.card_line: Write a short legacy page of your values, stories and a skill to pass on.
titles.end_state: You will have written down the sayings and habits you picked up from people before you, and three stories from your own life worth telling. You will have named a skill you could teach and found someone who might like to learn it. By week six you will have shared one story or skill and written a short legacy page to keep or give away. It is a page of your own words.
who_for: People who want to pass something on
Grandparents, parents and mentors
Anyone who would like to write down their stories

letters.title: A welcome from Theodora Valdez-Brennan
letters.body: {first_name}, welcome. A legacy does not have to be large. This workbook asks for stories, sayings and one skill. Begin with the sayings and habits you picked up from the people before you.

letters.title: A note for week 2
letters.body: {first_name}, choose three stories from your own life. They need not be grand. Write each one as you would tell it to a friend.

letters.title: A note for week 4
letters.body: {first_name}, the values behind your choices come next. Write them in your own words. Keep each one to a sentence.

letters.title: A note for week 6
letters.body: {first_name}, thank you for finishing. Share one story or skill with someone this week. Your legacy page is yours to keep or to give away.

titles.card_line: Rebuild your weekly routine and make the new place feel like yours.
titles.end_state: You will have written down what has changed, without judging it, and made a short list of people and services you can call on. You will have a weekly routine for meals, sleep times and money admin. You will also have a new place that feels more like yours, one corner at a time. The workbook points you to proper legal advice for paperwork. At the end you will have a plan for the next season.
who_for: People starting over in a new home after a separation
Anyone rebuilding ordinary routines
Readers who want plain, practical steps

letters.title: A welcome from Isla MacPhail-Osei
letters.body: {first_name}, welcome. A smaller flat can feel very quiet after a separation, as I found myself. This workbook takes it slowly. Start by writing down what has changed, without judging any of it.

letters.title: A note for week 2
letters.body: {first_name}, a short list of people and services you can call on is useful in any week. Add numbers and addresses. If things feel too much, Help now is at the top of every screen.

letters.title: A note for week 4
letters.body: {first_name}, your weekly routine comes next: meals, sleep times and money admin. Keep it simple. A routine is a frame for the week, and you may change it.

letters.title: A note for week 6
letters.body: {first_name}, paperwork can feel heavy. This workbook points you to proper legal advice, and no more. Take it a page at a time and ask for help where you need it.

letters.title: A note for week 8
letters.body: {first_name}, thank you for the eight weeks. Look back over what you have done. Plan the next season, and leave room in it for something you want to try.

titles.card_line: Decide what you want from dating, and meet someone for coffee at your own pace.
titles.end_state: You will have written down what you want from dating now and what you do not. You will have the basics for staying safe: a public place, a friend who knows, and your own way home. You will have a short, honest introduction and a plan for a first coffee, including a polite way to end it. By week six you will have chosen your own pace and when to stop for a while.
who_for: People dating again after a long time
Anyone who wants to go slowly
Readers who like clear safety basics

letters.title: A welcome from Isla MacPhail-Osei
letters.body: {first_name}, welcome. Dating again can feel strange, and there is no rush. This workbook starts with what you want and what you do not. Write both lists honestly.

letters.title: A note for week 2
letters.body: {first_name}, safety comes first. Meet in a public place, tell a friend where you are and plan your own way home. These are sensible habits for anyone.

letters.title: A note for week 4
letters.body: {first_name}, a first meeting over coffee is enough. Decide in advance how you will end it politely. A short, kind sentence is all you need.

letters.title: A note for week 6
letters.body: {first_name}, thank you for the six weeks. Your pace is your own. You can stop for a while, and start again when you want to.

titles.card_line: Write a few plain sentences for telling people about a separation.
titles.end_state: You will have listed who needs to know and in what order. You will have a few plain sentences you can repeat, including for children, and ready replies to questions, opinions and well-meant advice. By week four you will also know what you want to keep private and how to say so. The words are your own, kept on one page. The workbook does not give legal advice.
who_for: People about to share news of a separation
Parents who need words for their children
Anyone dreading the questions that follow

letters.title: A welcome from Clodagh Ní Fhaoláin-Burke
letters.body: {first_name}, welcome. Telling people is often harder than deciding. This workbook gives you time to prepare. Start with a list of who needs to know and the order you will tell them.

letters.title: A note for week 2
letters.body: {first_name}, write a few plain sentences you can repeat. Keep them short and true. For children, choose words that fit their age, and say the same thing each time.

letters.title: A note for week 3
letters.body: {first_name}, questions and advice will come. Prepare a polite reply for each kind. You may say that you would rather not talk about it.

letters.title: A note for week 4
letters.body: {first_name}, thank you for finishing. Decide what stays private and write down how you will say so. If a week feels too heavy, Help now is at the top of every screen.

titles.card_line: Keep weekly notes through the first year and a list of who to call for what.
titles.end_state: You will have a notebook that follows the first year, week by week. You will have a list of who to call for what, including your health visitor or doctor. You will also have a fair split of night and day jobs. You will have small routines, questions for your health checks and notes on how you are doing, as well as the baby. At the end there is a look back at the year and a note to yourself.
who_for: New parents who like a list and a plan
Partners sharing the first year
Anyone who wants a record to look back on

letters.title: A welcome from Ffion Rees-Adeyemi
letters.body: {first_name}, welcome. My notebooks from two first years are among the things I treasure. This workbook gives you a structure for yours. Start with the first days at home and the people around you.

letters.title: A note for week 3
letters.body: {first_name}, a list of who to call for what is gold in the early weeks. Add your health visitor or doctor. Keep it by the phone.

letters.title: A note for week 6
letters.body: {first_name}, this is the week to prepare for your health check. Write down the questions for your next health check as they occur to you. Bring the list along.

letters.title: A note for week 9
letters.body: {first_name}, how are you doing, not only how is the baby? This is the week to write it down. If things feel hard, speak to your health visitor or doctor.

letters.title: A note for week 12
letters.body: {first_name}, thank you for the twelve weeks. Look back over the year and write a note to yourself. Put in a photograph or two.

titles.card_line: Plan your first Monday back at work hour by hour.
titles.end_state: You will have written down what you want your return to work to look like. You will have looked at childcare options, drop-offs and a backup plan, and prepared for a conversation with your manager about the first weeks. By week four you will have written out the first Monday hour by hour, and planned a review afterwards. The plan is one set of pages you can share with your partner or your manager.
who_for: Parents returning to work after leave
Partners sharing drop-offs and backup plans
Anyone dreading the first Monday

letters.title: A welcome from Ffion Rees-Adeyemi
letters.body: {first_name}, welcome. The first Monday back is easier when it is planned. This workbook helps you write the plan. Begin with what you want your return to look like.

letters.title: A note for week 2
letters.body: {first_name}, childcare, drop-offs and a backup plan are next. Write down who does what, and who steps in when someone is ill.

letters.title: A note for week 3
letters.body: {first_name}, prepare for the talk with your manager. Write your questions down. Ask about the first weeks and what is flexible.

letters.title: A note for week 4
letters.body: {first_name}, the first Monday is here. Write out the hours and keep the plan close. Review how it went at the end of the week, and adjust.

titles.card_line: Choose two baby jobs to own from start to finish and review the split.
titles.end_state: You will have listed every baby and home job and who does it now. You will have chosen two whole jobs to own from start to finish. You will have spent time alone with the baby, writing down what you learn from it. You will have talked with your partner about how the week is going and found other fathers or friends for support. By week six you will have reviewed the split and planned the next three months.
who_for: New fathers who want to share the early months equally
Partners who want a fairer split of baby jobs
Anyone looking for support from other fathers

letters.title: A welcome from Jamal Whitacre-Odom
letters.body: {first_name}, welcome. As the father of twins, I learned that sharing the early months only works if you own jobs, not tasks. This workbook starts with a list of every baby and home job and who does it now.

letters.title: A note for week 2
letters.body: {first_name}, choose two whole jobs to own from start to finish. That includes noticing when they need doing. Tell your partner which two you have chosen.

letters.title: A note for week 4
letters.body: {first_name}, time alone with the baby teaches you things no instruction can. Write down what you notice. Talk to your partner about how the week is going.

letters.title: A note for week 6
letters.body: {first_name}, thank you for finishing. Review the split together and plan the next three months. Fathers need support too, so keep in touch with other fathers.

titles.card_line: Agree a few house rules between the adults and make time for each child.
titles.end_state: You will have a clear picture of who lives in your house, who visits and what each person calls the others. You will have talked through what each adult brings from their old household, and agreed a few house rules between the adults first. You will have set aside one-to-one time for each parent with their own children, and begun new traditions alongside old ones. A family meeting at the end checks what has settled.
who_for: Adults forming a stepfamily
Step-parents unsure of their role
Parents who want to keep children out of the middle

letters.title: A welcome from Sofia Hedlund-Ahl
letters.body: {first_name}, welcome. A stepfamily takes time. This workbook starts with a plain picture: who lives here, who visits and what each person is called. Draw it together if you can.

letters.title: A note for week 2
letters.body: {first_name}, the adults agree house rules first. Talk privately and decide together before telling the children. A united approach spares everyone confusion.

letters.title: A note for week 4
letters.body: {first_name}, the step-parent's role is delicate. Take a back seat while the relationships grow. Let the parent lead on discipline, and offer warmth in your own way.

letters.title: A note for week 6
letters.body: {first_name}, the other household matters too. Speak kindly about it in front of the children. Keep them out of the middle of any dispute.

letters.title: A note for week 8
letters.body: {first_name}, thank you for the eight weeks. Hold a family meeting and ask what has settled and what has not. Keep a few old traditions and add a new one.

titles.card_line: Set a weekly routine for school, meals and bedtimes and a list of who can help.
titles.end_state: You will have a picture of what has changed in your house and what each person needs. You will have a weekly routine for school, meals and bedtimes, and a support list of family, school, local services and other kinship carers. You will have found words for telling the children why they are here, fitted to their age. The workbook points to official help on money and paperwork, and ends with time for yourself.
who_for: Grandparents and relatives raising children
Carers who stepped in at short notice
Anyone who needs a plain routine and a support list

letters.title: A welcome from Mereana Tautahi-Cole
letters.body: {first_name}, welcome. When my grandchildren came to stay, nothing in the house was ready. This workbook takes it a step at a time. Begin by writing down what has changed and who needs what.

letters.title: A note for week 2
letters.body: {first_name}, a weekly routine for school, meals and bedtimes gives the children a steady frame. Keep it simple, and write it where they can see it.

letters.title: A note for week 4
letters.body: {first_name}, a support list is worth building now. Add family, school, local services and other kinship carers. You are not doing this alone.

letters.title: A note for week 6
letters.body: {first_name}, thank you for finishing. Money and paperwork can wait for a calm hour, and this workbook points you to official help. Make time for yourself and decide who to ask for help next.

titles.card_line: Agree a regular day or call with the parents and keep one tradition going.
titles.end_state: You will have written down the time you have with your grandchildren now and what you would like it to be. You will have had a talk with the parents about their rules and yours. You will have agreed a regular day or call, in person or from a distance. By week four you will have chosen small traditions and stories to pass on. The workbook is about staying close without taking over.
who_for: Grandparents who want to stay close
Families agreeing who does what
Anyone who lives far from the grandchildren

letters.title: A welcome from Mereana Tautahi-Cole
letters.body: {first_name}, welcome. Being a grandparent is a gift, and it works best when the parents are on side. This workbook starts with what you have now and what you would like.

letters.title: A note for week 2
letters.body: {first_name}, talk with the parents about their rules and yours. Listen first. It is their house and their children, and they will welcome your help more if you ask.

letters.title: A note for week 3
letters.body: {first_name}, a regular day or call gives children a fixed point in their week. Choose a time that suits everyone, and keep to it.

letters.title: A note for week 4
letters.body: {first_name}, thank you for finishing. Choose a tradition or a story to pass on. Write it down so that it is not lost.

titles.card_line: Set up one care folder and share the jobs with the people around you.
titles.end_state: You will have one folder for contacts, appointments and letters, and a ten-minute weekly check of the folder and the diary. You will have a list of questions for appointments and specific requests for help from family and friends. You will also have talked with your parent about what they want. Over twelve weeks you will also plan for your own work, health and rest. The workbook points to official guidance on money and forms.
who_for: People looking after a parent or relative
Carers who handle the appointments and paperwork
Anyone sharing care with brothers, sisters or friends

letters.title: A welcome from Rukhsana Begum-Thornley
letters.body: {first_name}, welcome. Looking after my father taught me how much of caring is planning and paperwork. This workbook helps you keep it in one place. Start with what care looks like now and who does each part.

letters.title: A note for week 3
letters.body: {first_name}, a single folder for contacts, appointments and letters saves hours. Set one up this week. Keep a weekly ten-minute check in your diary.

letters.title: A note for week 6
letters.body: {first_name}, asking for help goes further when you are specific. Name the task, the day and the person. Brothers, sisters and friends often want to help and do not know how.

letters.title: A note for week 9
letters.body: {first_name}, money and forms are a chore, and this workbook points you to official guidance. Take them one page at a time. Your own job and hours matter too.

letters.title: A note for week 12
letters.body: {first_name}, thank you for the twelve weeks. Review the folder and the share of jobs. Keep a backup plan for when you cannot be there, and look after your own health.

titles.card_line: Book one afternoon to yourself and make breaks a regular part of caring.
titles.end_state: You will have looked at when you last had time off and what got in the way. You will have a short list of who could cover, and the local respite or day services to ask about. You will have booked one afternoon for yourself and planned how to spend it. By week four you will have made the break regular and asked for the next one. It is a plan for rest, written for people who look after someone.
who_for: People who look after a relative or friend
Carers who have not had time off in months
Anyone who finds it hard to ask for cover

letters.title: A welcome from Rukhsana Begum-Thornley
letters.body: {first_name}, welcome. Carers often put themselves last. This workbook asks for one afternoon. Begin by writing down when you last had time off and what got in the way.

letters.title: A note for week 2
letters.body: {first_name}, who could cover for you? Write down every name, and ask about local respite or day services. Most areas offer something.

letters.title: A note for week 3
letters.body: {first_name}, book the afternoon this week, and plan how to spend it. Choose something you enjoy. You are allowed to rest.

letters.title: A note for week 4
letters.body: {first_name}, thank you for finishing. Make the break regular and ask for the next one before the last has ended.

titles.card_line: Bring photos, music and objects to visits and go along with the moment.
titles.end_state: You will have looked at what visits are like now and what you both enjoy. You will have a few photos, pieces of music and objects that start a conversation. You will have a habit of going along with the moment rather than correcting. You will have settled on short visits at regular times and shared visits with family and friends. You will also have a way of looking after yourself after a hard visit. The workbook gives no medical advice.
who_for: Relatives visiting someone whose memory is changing
Anyone unsure what to say on a visit
Family members who share the visits

letters.title: A welcome from Declan Hennessy-Ruane
letters.body: {first_name}, welcome. Most evenings in her last years, I visited my mother. Some visits were easy, and some were not. This workbook begins with what visits are like now and what you both enjoy.

letters.title: A note for week 2
letters.body: {first_name}, photos, music and familiar objects can start a conversation. Choose a few and take them with you. You need not use them all.

letters.title: A note for week 4
letters.body: {first_name}, going along with the moment is kinder than correcting. If a memory is wrong, let it be. Share the feeling in it.

letters.title: A note for week 6
letters.body: {first_name}, thank you for finishing. Look after yourself after a hard visit. Sit for a few minutes before you go home, and talk to someone who understands.

titles.card_line: Build and give a five-minute talk around one point.
titles.end_state: You will have chosen one point and built a five-minute talk around it. You will have practised out loud, with notes you can glance at, and found ordinary ways to handle nerves. By week six you will have given the talk, taken questions and asked for one piece of feedback. The result is a talk you can give again, and a method for the next one that fits on a single page.
who_for: People asked to give a short talk at work
Anyone who dreads the front of the room
Quiet colleagues who want to be heard

letters.title: A welcome from Priya Sandhu-Lavoie
letters.body: {first_name}, welcome. On community radio I learned that a talk is built around one point. This workbook helps you choose yours and build five minutes around it.

letters.title: A note for week 2
letters.body: {first_name}, practise out loud this week. Use notes you can glance at, not read. Nerves are normal, and ordinary habits like a glass of water and a slow start will do.

letters.title: A note for week 4
letters.body: {first_name}, give your talk. Take questions, and ask one person for a piece of feedback. Thank you for the care you have taken.

letters.title: A note for week 6
letters.body: {first_name}, the talk is behind you. Keep the notes and the method. Next time, begin with the one point.

titles.card_line: Prepare a request, trade fairly and write the agreement down.
titles.end_state: You will have worked out what you want, what the other side wants and your walk-away point. You will have practised opening clearly, listening and trading instead of just conceding. You will have tried practice rounds on a supplier, a deadline and a workload request, and written the agreement down. By week eight you will have reviewed how it went. It is a method for ordinary asks, with no tricks.
who_for: People who need to ask for a better deal at work
Anyone who gives way too quickly
Buyers, suppliers and colleagues who want fair agreements

letters.title: A welcome from Lamar Whitfield-Osei
letters.body: {first_name}, welcome. A decade of coaching debate taught me that fair asking is a skill. This workbook starts with what you want, what they want and your walk-away point.

letters.title: A note for week 2
letters.body: {first_name}, opening clearly is half the work. State your request in a sentence. Then listen. Trade something you can spare for something you need.

letters.title: A note for week 4
letters.body: {first_name}, practice rounds come next. Try them with a friend on a supplier, a deadline and a workload request. Swap roles and see how it feels.

letters.title: A note for week 6
letters.body: {first_name}, write the agreement down and send it to the other side. A short note avoids later confusion. Then review how it went.

letters.title: A note for week 8
letters.body: {first_name}, thank you for the eight weeks. Keep your notes and use them before the next negotiation. Asking well becomes a habit.

titles.card_line: Welcome a new starter with a buddy, a desk and a plan for the first month.
titles.end_state: You will have a welcome plan for a new team member, from the note before day one to a month-one conversation. It covers a buddy, a desk and a plain welcome, introductions in the first week and one small early win. You will also have written down the unwritten rules of your team so that a newcomer can read them. At the end you note what to change for the next starter.
who_for: Team leads with a new starter on the way
Buddies and colleagues asked to help someone settle
Anyone who remembers a poor first week

letters.title: A welcome from Tama Rāwiri-Hughes
letters.body: {first_name}, welcome. Years of leading volunteer teams taught me that the first week sets the tone. This workbook gives you a plan for it. Start with the note before day one, a buddy and a desk.

letters.title: A note for week 2
letters.body: {first_name}, the first week needs introductions and one small early win. Plan both. A newcomer who finishes something in the first days stands a little taller.

letters.title: A note for week 3
letters.body: {first_name}, check in this week and invite questions without judgement. Write down the unwritten rules of your team. They are easy to forget, and hard for a newcomer to guess.

letters.title: A note for week 4
letters.body: {first_name}, thank you for finishing. Hold the month-one conversation, and ask what you could do better for the next starter. Write it down while it is fresh.

titles.card_line: Write a one-page team agreement for office days and home days.
titles.end_state: You will have a clear idea of what each kind of day is for and what people need from each. You will have settled how meetings and messages work, and a way to make sure remote voices are heard. By week six you will have a one-page team agreement and a date to review it. The agreement is written with the team, so it reflects how people really work. It does not give legal or employment advice.
who_for: Team leads running a mix of office and home days
Colleagues who want fairer ways of working
Small firms setting up hybrid working for the first time

letters.title: A welcome from Mei-Lin Gallagher-Ross
letters.body: {first_name}, welcome. Two moves and a switch to hybrid working taught me that clear habits matter more than clever policies. This workbook starts with what each kind of day is for.

letters.title: A note for week 2
letters.body: {first_name}, meetings and messages are where hybrid teams struggle. This week you agree how they work, and how to make sure those at home are heard as well as those in the room.

letters.title: A note for week 4
letters.body: {first_name}, draft the one-page agreement with the team, not for it. Keep it short. Include a date to review it.

letters.title: A note for week 6
letters.body: {first_name}, thank you for finishing. Review the agreement on the date you set, and change what has not worked. For employment questions, ask a qualified adviser.

titles.card_line: Draw up a team charter in which everyone speaks and is heard.
titles.end_state: Over twelve weeks your team will have noticed who speaks, who does not and why. You will have tried turn-taking, written input and room for quieter people, and practised disagreeing well, admitting mistakes and thanking people for raising them. You will also have fairer hiring and welcome habits. The programme ends with a team charter that everyone has helped to write and agreed to keep.
who_for: Teams who want every voice heard in meetings
Leaders who want fairer ways of working
Groups that will work through the programme together

letters.title: A welcome from Mei-Lin Gallagher-Ross
letters.body: {first_name}, welcome. A meeting that only a few people speak in wastes the others. This programme is for a whole team, working together. Start by noticing who speaks, who does not, and why.

letters.title: A note for week 3
letters.body: {first_name}, turn-taking and written input are next. They give quieter people room. Try them for a few weeks and ask the team what they notice.

letters.title: A note for week 6
letters.body: {first_name}, disagreeing well is a skill. Thank people for raising problems, and admit your own mistakes first. It makes it safer for everyone else.

letters.title: A note for week 9
letters.body: {first_name}, fair hiring and welcome habits close the programme. Think about who you ask to join and how you greet them.

letters.title: A note for week 12
letters.body: {first_name}, thank you for the twelve weeks. Write the team charter together and sign it. Review it every six months.

titles.card_line: Write and send a monthly newsletter that your customers want to open.
titles.end_state: You will have decided who your newsletter is for, what they want to hear and how you ask permission to email them. You will have a simple template and a first issue written. You will have clear subject lines, one offer in each issue and plain unsubscribe wording. By week four you will have a three-month plan of topics and a time in the diary to write. The workbook gives no legal advice, so check the email rules that apply to you.
who_for: Owners of small shops and businesses
Anyone with a list of customers and no plan
People who dislike selling and prefer to be useful

letters.title: A welcome from Niamh Oyelaran-Byrne
letters.body: {first_name}, welcome. A newsletter should read like a letter from a friendly shop, not an advert. This workbook starts with who it is for, what they want to hear and how you ask permission.

letters.title: A note for week 2
letters.body: {first_name}, a simple template saves time. Write your first issue this week. Keep it short, kind and useful.

letters.title: A note for week 3
letters.body: {first_name}, subject lines and offers come next. Write a clear subject line, make one offer and add plain unsubscribe wording. Check the email rules that apply to your business.

letters.title: A note for week 4
letters.body: {first_name}, thank you for finishing. Plan three months of topics and put a writing slot in your diary. A newsletter is kept going by a routine.

titles.card_line: Hold honest sales conversations and keep a simple log of them.
titles.end_state: You will have written down what you sell, who it helps and who it does not. You will have practised listening first, asking good questions and stating the price plainly. You will have a follow-up routine, a calm reply to not now, and a habit of staying honest. By week eight you will keep a simple sales log and review it each month. It is a method for small firms that prefer conversation to pressure.
who_for: Owners of small firms who dislike selling
Anyone who feels awkward stating a price
People who want a plain, honest sales routine

letters.title: A welcome from Niamh Oyelaran-Byrne
letters.body: {first_name}, welcome. In a small shop, selling is just talking to a neighbour. This workbook builds on that. Begin by writing what you sell, who it helps and who it does not.

letters.title: A note for week 2
letters.body: {first_name}, listening first is the whole trick. Ask good questions and let the customer finish. Then say the price plainly and wait.

letters.title: A note for week 4
letters.body: {first_name}, follow-up is where small firms lose sales. Plan it, and handle not now with grace. Stay honest about what you can and cannot do.

letters.title: A note for week 6
letters.body: {first_name}, a simple sales log shows you what is working. Keep it brief. Note the name, the date and what happened.

letters.title: A note for week 8
letters.body: {first_name}, thank you for the eight weeks. Review the log each month and adjust. Keep your conversations kind, and your promises small.

titles.card_line: List everything you owe on one page and know who to call for debt advice.
titles.end_state: You will have gathered your statements and letters at your own pace, pausing whenever you need to. You will have one page that lists who you owe, how much and the minimum payment. You will also have a clear order of priority bills, such as rent, council tax and energy. By week four you will know where independent debt advice is available and have the details to book a conversation if you want one. The workbook gives no personal financial advice.
who_for: People who have avoided looking at what they owe
Anyone facing letters from lenders
Readers who want a calm, step-by-step first look

letters.title: A welcome from Rhiannon Asante-Pugh
letters.body: {first_name}, welcome. Owing money is common, and you need not carry it with shame. This workbook is gentle. Gather your papers at your own pace, and stop whenever you need to.

letters.title: A note for week 2
letters.body: {first_name}, the one-page list is the core of this workbook. Write who you owe, how much and the minimum payment. The page may be uncomfortable to see. It is also a place to begin.

letters.title: A note for week 3
letters.body: {first_name}, some bills matter more than others, such as rent, council tax and energy. Mark them. If you feel overwhelmed, Help now is at the top of every screen.

letters.title: A note for week 4
letters.body: {first_name}, thank you for finishing. Independent debt advice exists and many services charge nothing. Keep the page up to date, and book a conversation if you want one.

titles.card_line: Work out what you can spare each month and compare two ways of ordering repayments.
titles.end_state: You will have a realistic budget and a figure you can spare each month. You will have compared two common ways of ordering repayments, with no recommendation made for you. You will have a plan for talking to lenders, a record-keeping habit and a nose for offers that sound too good. By week eight you will have thought through tight months and small setbacks, and know when to ask an independent debt advice service for support.
who_for: People paying down debts at a steady pace
Anyone who wants a notebook to track repayments
Readers who want to understand their options without being told what to do

letters.title: A welcome from Rhiannon Asante-Pugh
letters.body: {first_name}, welcome. A repayment notebook keeps the numbers in front of you. Begin with a realistic budget and the amount you can spare each month. Be honest, not hopeful.

letters.title: A note for week 2
letters.body: {first_name}, there are common ways of ordering repayments. This workbook compares two and recommends neither. The right choice depends on your own situation.

letters.title: A note for week 4
letters.body: {first_name}, talking to lenders is easier with records. Keep a log of each call and letter. Be wary of offers that sound too good to be true.

letters.title: A note for week 6
letters.body: {first_name}, tight months will come. Plan for them now. If you need support, independent debt advice services can talk through your situation.

letters.title: A note for week 8
letters.body: {first_name}, thank you for the eight weeks. Keep the notebook going. Steady steps add up, however small.

titles.card_line: Open the post with a plan and keep a call log for every conversation.
titles.end_state: You will have opened your post with a plan, sorted your letters and noted the dates. You will understand, in general terms, what reminders, final demands and arrears letters usually mean. You will have written scripts for phone calls and letters, and a call log to keep. By week six you will also know where to find independent advice. The workbook explains in general terms and does not give personal financial advice.
who_for: People who have stopped opening their post
Anyone who dreads phone calls with lenders
Readers who want scripts and a plan

letters.title: A welcome from Tomasz Kowalczyk-Hale
letters.body: {first_name}, welcome. Falling behind on rent and council tax once left my own post piled up. This workbook gives you a plan for opening it. Choose a calm hour and a clear table.

letters.title: A note for week 2
letters.body: {first_name}, reminders, final demands and arrears letters mean different things. This week you learn, in general terms, what they usually say. Your own case may differ, so read each letter fully.

letters.title: A note for week 4
letters.body: {first_name}, scripts help on the phone. Write down what you want to say and what you want to ask. Keep a call log: the date, the name and what was agreed.

letters.title: A note for week 6
letters.body: {first_name}, thank you for finishing. Independent advice services will talk through your situation. Keep your log and your letters in one folder.

titles.card_line: Read your pension letters line by line and write your questions for the provider.
titles.end_state: You will know what a workplace pension is, how contributions and tax relief work in general terms, and how to look for old pots. You will be able to read an annual statement, spot charges and see the default fund. By week six you will have checked your State Pension forecast and written questions for your provider. The workbook points to MoneyHelper and Pension Wise for guidance and gives no personal advice.
who_for: Employees with a workplace pension they have never read
Anyone who has changed jobs and lost track of old pots
Readers who want plain words, not jargon

letters.title: A welcome from Iona Bhattacharya-Reid
letters.body: {first_name}, welcome. For years I answered colleagues' questions about payslips and pension letters. The same worry came up: what does this mean? This workbook reads those letters slowly with you.

letters.title: A note for week 2
letters.body: {first_name}, an annual statement shows what has gone in, what it costs and what it is invested in. This week you read yours line by line. Mark anything you do not understand.

letters.title: A note for week 4
letters.body: {first_name}, check your State Pension forecast this week. Write your questions for your provider. MoneyHelper and Pension Wise offer guidance, and this workbook does not give personal advice.

letters.title: A note for week 6
letters.body: {first_name}, thank you for finishing. Keep your statements together and read them each year. A short annual look is a good habit.

titles.card_line: Understand how saving, pensions and investing work, and write your own questions first.
titles.end_state: You will understand cash savings, an emergency fund and why time matters, with made-up numbers to show how compounding works. You will know what shares, bonds and funds are, explained and not recommended. You will have read about pensions and ISAs in general terms, and learned to check a firm on the FCA register. By the end you will have your own questions written for a regulated adviser or free guidance service.
who_for: People who want to understand saving and investing
Anyone who feels lost when money terms are used
Readers who want to know the right questions to ask

letters.title: A welcome from Iona Bhattacharya-Reid
letters.body: {first_name}, welcome. This workbook explains how saving and investing work. It does not tell you what to buy. Start with cash savings and an emergency fund. Everything else builds on them.

letters.title: A note for week 3
letters.body: {first_name}, this week you meet shares, bonds and funds. The numbers in this workbook are made up. Their purpose is to show how the ideas work.

letters.title: A note for week 6
letters.body: {first_name}, pensions and ISAs come next, in general terms. Check any firm on the FCA register before you hand over money. Look at charges, as they matter over a long time.

letters.title: A note for week 9
letters.body: {first_name}, risk, losses and scams are the last part. Investments can fall as well as rise. Write your own questions before you speak to a regulated adviser.

letters.title: A note for week 12
letters.body: {first_name}, thank you for the twelve weeks. Keep your list of questions. Guidance services can talk to you about your own circumstances.

titles.card_line: Spot the signs of a scam and know exactly what to do if one reaches you.
titles.end_state: You will know how scams reach people, by call, text, email and advert. You will know the pressure signs to watch for, such as urgency, secrecy and odd ways to pay. You will check a message or caller using contact details you already hold. You will have stronger passwords, two-step checks and updates on your own devices. By week six you will have your own plan for what to do and who to tell if something goes wrong.
who_for: Anyone who gets odd calls, texts and emails
People who help a parent or friend online
Readers who want plain, practical steps

letters.title: A welcome from Priya Ramdhanie-Cole
letters.body: {first_name}, welcome. At my library drop-in, many people feel foolish about scams, and they should not. Scammers are skilled. This workbook shows how they reach you, and what to do.

letters.title: A note for week 2
letters.body: {first_name}, the pressure signs are the key. Urgency, secrecy and odd ways to pay are red flags. This week you learn to pause before you act.

letters.title: A note for week 4
letters.body: {first_name}, look after your own devices this week. Choose strong passwords, switch on two-step checks and update your software. It takes less time than you expect.

letters.title: A note for week 6
letters.body: {first_name}, thank you for finishing. Write your own plan for what to do and who to tell if something goes wrong. Keep it by the phone.

titles.card_line: Notice when you pick up your phone and keep the changes you liked.
titles.end_state: You will have noticed, for a plain week, when and why you pick up your phone. You will have changed your notifications and home screen, and thought about the apps that pull hardest. You will have phone-free times and places that suit your household. By week four you will look back at the month and keep the changes you liked. There are no screen-time targets, and nobody is scored.
who_for: People who reach for the phone without thinking
Households who want phone-free times
Readers who want small, practical changes

letters.title: A welcome from Priya Ramdhanie-Cole
letters.body: {first_name}, welcome. Our phones are useful and they are hard to put down. This workbook begins with noticing, for a week, when and why you pick yours up. No changes yet.

letters.title: A note for week 2
letters.body: {first_name}, notifications and home screens are next. Switch off what you do not need and move the apps that pull hardest. A small change on the screen makes a surprising difference.

letters.title: A note for week 3
letters.body: {first_name}, choose phone-free times and places for your household. A meal, a bedroom, a walk. Agree them together and write them down.

letters.title: A note for week 4
letters.body: {first_name}, thank you for finishing. Keep the changes you liked. Drop the rest and do not feel guilty about it.

titles.card_line: Build simple spreadsheets for your bills, meals and household jobs.
titles.end_state: You will have made a first list of household jobs using rows and columns, and a sheet of regular bills with simple sums. You will have a meal and shopping planner that you can sort and filter. By week four you will have shared a sheet with your household and learned to keep it tidy. Each sheet is small and made for a real home. No earlier experience of spreadsheets is needed.
who_for: People new to spreadsheets
Housemates and families who share costs and jobs
Anyone who wants to tidy household paperwork

letters.title: A welcome from Matilda Kershaw-Nguyen
letters.body: {first_name}, welcome. Spreadsheets look fearsome, but a good one is just a tidy list. This workbook starts with rows, columns and a first list of household jobs.

letters.title: A note for week 2
letters.body: {first_name}, simple sums come next. Enter your regular bills and add them up. Let the sheet do the arithmetic, and check it once against your own.

letters.title: A note for week 3
letters.body: {first_name}, a meal and shopping planner uses sorting and filters. These are small tools with big effects. Try them on your own list.

letters.title: A note for week 4
letters.body: {first_name}, thank you for finishing. Share your sheet with your household and keep it tidy. A shared sheet only works if everyone keeps it up to date.

titles.card_line: Plan a children's group session in four parts and share the plan with other volunteers.
titles.end_state: You will have a clear picture of who comes to your group, what they need and what you hope they take home. You will have a simple session shape of welcome, story, activity and close, and plans for mixed ages and for children who find groups hard. You will know how to share the plan with other volunteers, and who to ask about keeping children safe under your organisation's rules. At the end you will have reviewed a term and planned the next.
who_for: Volunteers who run groups for children
Parents asked to help at a club or Sunday group
Anyone planning sessions for mixed ages

letters.title: A welcome from Aoife Brannigan-Oduya
letters.body: {first_name}, welcome. On Sunday mornings I plan sessions around a simple shape. This workbook gives you the same shape. Begin by writing who comes, what they need and what you hope they take home.

letters.title: A note for week 2
letters.body: {first_name}, plan for mixed ages and for children who find groups hard. Offer a quiet corner and a choice of activity. Small adjustments help children feel they belong.

letters.title: A note for week 4
letters.body: {first_name}, safety comes first. Read your organisation's rules and know who to ask. This workbook does not replace your safeguarding training.

letters.title: A note for week 6
letters.body: {first_name}, thank you for finishing. Review the term with your fellow volunteers and plan the next. Keep the session shape on a single card.

titles.card_line: Run a first tutoring session and plan short sessions with exercises and review.
titles.end_state: You will have held a first session, getting to know the learner and what they want. You will have found out what they already know without a test that worries them. You will have planned short sessions that include exercises and review, and talked with the learner or their parents about progress and next steps. The workbook is for new tutors and fits around a busy week.
who_for: New tutors working with one learner
Parents and students who tutor others
Anyone who wants a plain plan for the first month

letters.title: A welcome from Olivier Tremblay-Singh
letters.body: {first_name}, welcome. Tutoring begins with the learner, not the subject. In this workbook, your first session is about getting to know them and what they want.

letters.title: A note for week 2
letters.body: {first_name}, find out what they already know without a test. Ask them to show you how they would solve a problem. Listen to the reasoning more than the answer.

letters.title: A note for week 3
letters.body: {first_name}, plan short sessions with exercises and review. Twenty minutes of focused work beats an hour of drifting. End each session with one thing they can say.

letters.title: A note for week 4
letters.body: {first_name}, thank you for finishing. Talk with the learner, or their parents, about progress and next steps. Keep your notes for the next block.

titles.card_line: Write for twenty minutes at the same time and place each day.
titles.end_state: You will have chosen a time, a place and a notebook, and written for twenty minutes a day. You will have tried free writing, writing from objects and memories, and writing scenes from overheard talk. You will have kept going on low-energy days with shorter sittings. You will have picked one piece to take further and read it aloud for a first revision. At the end you will look back at your pages and set the next eight weeks.
who_for: People who want to write regularly
Anyone fitting a writing habit around a full life
Readers who like a notebook and a plain plan

letters.title: A welcome from Marisol Abernathy-Kwan
letters.body: {first_name}, welcome. A writing group in Tucson taught me that a habit beats inspiration. This workbook asks for twenty minutes a day. Choose a time, a place and a notebook.

letters.title: A note for week 2
letters.body: {first_name}, write from objects and memories around the house this week. Pick up a spoon, a key, a photograph. Write what comes. Do not judge it.

letters.title: A note for week 4
letters.body: {first_name}, low-energy days will come. Write for five minutes, or one sentence. A smaller sitting still counts as a sitting.

letters.title: A note for week 6
letters.body: {first_name}, choose one piece to take further. Read it aloud and mark the lines that sound wrong. Make a first revision.

letters.title: A note for week 8
letters.body: {first_name}, thank you for the eight weeks. Look back at your pages. Set the next eight weeks, and keep the same time and place.

titles.card_line: Draft, revise and finish three short stories and share one with a reader.
titles.end_state: You will have read short stories as a writer and kept a list of ideas. You will have drafted your first story and built a character with a want, a fear and one telling detail. You will have worked on setting, point of view, openings, endings and dialogue. You will have revised for shape and line by line, drafted a second and third story, and shared one with a reader. At the end you choose what to send out.
who_for: Writers who want to finish short fiction
Anyone who starts stories and abandons them
Members of a writing group who want a shared plan

letters.title: A welcome from Marisol Abernathy-Kwan
letters.body: {first_name}, welcome. Finishing a short story is a skill, and this season is built to help you finish. Begin by reading stories as a writer, and keep an idea list.

letters.title: A note for week 3
letters.body: {first_name}, you have started your first story. Character comes first: a want, a fear and one telling detail. Keep the draft rough and keep moving.

letters.title: A note for week 6
letters.body: {first_name}, openings and endings shape the whole story. Write three versions of each. Choose the one that feels truest.

letters.title: A note for week 9
letters.body: {first_name}, revising is where stories are made. This week, cut and move scenes for shape. Next week, work line by line.

letters.title: A note for week 12
letters.body: {first_name}, thank you for the twelve weeks. Share a story with a reader, take their feedback and choose what to send out. Keep writing.

titles.card_line: Record a family member telling their stories and share a short clip with consent.
titles.end_state: You will have chosen who to record and asked them kindly. You will have a phone, a quiet room and a simple set-up, and questions that open stories up. You will have practised listening well, following up and knowing when to stop. By week six you will have labelled, stored and backed up your recordings and shared a short clip with your family, with the speaker's consent. The result is a small archive of voices.
who_for: People with relatives whose stories should be kept
Anyone who loves radio and oral history
Families who want a keepsake in voices

letters.title: A welcome from Rafael Moreira Lins
letters.body: {first_name}, welcome. A voice carries more than a page can. This workbook helps you record a family story. Begin by choosing who to record and asking them kindly.

letters.title: A note for week 2
letters.body: {first_name}, a phone and a quiet room are enough. Test your set-up with a short recording. Listen back and adjust before the real one.

letters.title: A note for week 4
letters.body: {first_name}, good questions open stories up. Ask about a place, a person or a day. Listen, follow up and know when to stop.

letters.title: A note for week 6
letters.body: {first_name}, thank you for finishing. Label, store and back up your recordings. Share a clip only with the speaker's consent.

titles.card_line: Start your family history with what you know and where each fact came from.
titles.end_state: You will have started with yourself, what you know and how you know it, and talked to older relatives. You will have sorted photographs, letters and papers, drawn a simple family tree and searched birth, marriage and death records and census returns. You will have checked facts and noted the source of each. By week twelve you will have turned names into stories, shared what you found and saved your work safely.
who_for: People starting a family history
Anyone with boxes of photographs and papers
Families who want to record stories while they can

letters.title: A welcome from Ailsa Fenwick-Dhillon
letters.body: {first_name}, welcome. Both sides of my family have been traced, and every discovery began with a conversation. This workbook starts with you: what you know and how you know it.

letters.title: A note for week 3
letters.body: {first_name}, talk to older relatives and record what they say. Ask permission first. Write the date and their name on each recording.

letters.title: A note for week 6
letters.body: {first_name}, birth, marriage and death records come next, then census returns. Note where each fact came from. A source turns a rumour into a record.

letters.title: A note for week 9
letters.body: {first_name}, surprises and difficult discoveries are part of the work. Handle them with care, and think before you share. Not every fact needs to be told to everyone.

letters.title: A note for week 12
letters.body: {first_name}, thank you for the twelve weeks. Keep your work safe, with copies in two places. Pass it on to someone who will care for it.

titles.card_line: Write letters to the people you love and decide when they are given.
titles.end_state: You will have chosen who to write to and what you want them to have. You will have written about memories you share, and about what matters to you and why. By week four you will have finished the letters, stored them somewhere safe and decided when they are given. The workbook asks for no more than a pen and paper. The letters belong to you and to the people they are for.
who_for: People who want to leave words for those they love
Grandparents, parents and friends
Anyone who finds it easier to write than to say

letters.title: A welcome from Ailsa Fenwick-Dhillon
letters.body: {first_name}, welcome. Some things are easier to write than to say. This workbook asks you to write letters, one at a time. Begin by choosing who to write to and what you want them to have.

letters.title: A note for week 2
letters.body: {first_name}, write about memories you share. Be specific: a day, a place, a small detail. These are the things people remember.

letters.title: A note for week 3
letters.body: {first_name}, this week you write about what matters to you and why. Take your time and use plain words. They will be read slowly.

letters.title: A note for week 4
letters.body: {first_name}, thank you for finishing. Store the letters safely and decide when they are given. Tell someone where they are kept.

titles.card_line: Make one small thing each week with materials you already own.
titles.end_state: You will have cleared a small space and gathered materials you already own. Over six weeks you will have made a small notebook from paper, learned three simple stitches, mended something you like and made a small gift. The last week looks back at the six things you made and chooses what to make next. Each project takes an hour or two, and nothing needs special tools.
who_for: People who want a creative habit without fuss
Beginners at sewing and paper craft
Anyone with a drawer of materials and no plan

letters.title: A welcome from Tessa Wyborn-Liang
letters.body: {first_name}, welcome. A craft habit starts small. This workbook asks for one thing a week. Clear a small space and gather the materials you already own.

letters.title: A note for week 2
letters.body: {first_name}, this week you learn three simple stitches. Practise on a scrap first. Make them neat, and then make them yours.

letters.title: A note for week 4
letters.body: {first_name}, mending is a form of making. Choose something you like and give it a second life. A visible repair is a pleasure.

letters.title: A note for week 6
letters.body: {first_name}, thank you for the six weeks. Look at the six things you have made and choose what to make next. Share one with someone.

titles.card_line: Choose ten photographs from your neighbourhood and make a small collection.
titles.end_state: You will have walked at a different time of day and looked at light. You will have photographed close up, with textures, plants and small details, and learned to ask before photographing someone. By week four you will have chosen ten photographs from your neighbourhood and made a small collection, printed or on screen. A phone camera is enough, and no earlier experience is needed.
who_for: People who want to look at their street with fresh eyes
Beginners with a phone camera
Anyone who enjoys a short walk with a purpose

letters.title: A welcome from Tessa Wyborn-Liang
letters.body: {first_name}, welcome. A camera makes you look. This workbook asks you to walk at a different time of day and notice the light. A phone camera is enough.

letters.title: A note for week 2
letters.body: {first_name}, this week you go close up. Look for textures, plants and small details. Take more photographs than you need and choose later.

letters.title: A note for week 3
letters.body: {first_name}, people and places make good pictures. Ask before you photograph someone, and respect a refusal. Make a short note of where you were.

letters.title: A note for week 4
letters.body: {first_name}, thank you for finishing. Choose ten photographs and put them together as a small collection. Share them with someone from your neighbourhood.

titles.card_line: Test Franklin's sayings on industry and thrift against your own week.
titles.end_state: You will have read Franklin's short piece, drawn from his almanac in 1758, in four parts. You will have tried his sayings on industry and thrift against your own week, kept the ones that fit and put the rest aside. By the end you will have a short page of your own sayings about time and money. You will also have a small habit from the piece that you have tested. Akana added the exercises. The text stays Franklin's.
who_for: Readers who like short, old and practical books
Anyone curious what thrift meant in 1758
People who want to test old advice on their own week

letters.title: A note from Akana about Benjamin Franklin
letters.body: {first_name}, welcome. This note comes from Akana, not from Benjamin Franklin. The piece you are about to read was first printed in 1758, a collection of sayings on industry and thrift. Akana has added the exercises, and Franklin's words stay his own.

letters.title: A note from Akana, week 2
letters.body: {first_name}, the sayings are short on purpose. They were made to be repeated. This week the exercises ask you to hold one against your own days and note what you find. Some will fit, and some will seem dated.

letters.title: A note from Akana, week 3
letters.body: {first_name}, notice which sayings sound wise and which sound harsh to a modern ear. Both reactions are worth writing down. Akana does not ask you to agree with all of it.

letters.title: A note from Akana, week 4
letters.body: {first_name}, this is the last week. Akana hopes you keep a few sayings that earned their place and a short list of your own. The piece is old, and the habit of testing it against life is the useful part.

titles.card_line: Read Smiles' short lives of patient effort and plan one of your own.
titles.end_state: You will have read selections from Smiles' 1859 book, with its short lives of people who worked patiently at difficult things. You will have noted what each life asks of a reader today and sorted what holds up from what belongs to its century. By week six you will have a plan for one piece of patient effort of your own, with steps and a date to review. Akana wrote the exercises and the notes. The text is Smiles' own.
who_for: Readers who enjoy Victorian life stories
Anyone planning a long, patient piece of work
People who want an old book with practical exercises

letters.title: A note from Akana about Samuel Smiles
letters.body: {first_name}, welcome. This note is from Akana, writing about Samuel Smiles. His book Self-Help appeared in 1859 and was among the best read of its time. Akana has chosen selections and written the exercises. The words you read are his.

letters.title: A note from Akana, week 2
letters.body: {first_name}, the lives in this book are chosen to show patient effort. Read each as a story first. Then ask what it would ask of you today, and what belongs to its own century.

letters.title: A note from Akana, week 4
letters.body: {first_name}, some of the attitudes in a Victorian book will sit oddly now. Akana suggests noting them without argument. The exercises ask what holds up, and what does not.

letters.title: A note from Akana, week 6
letters.body: {first_name}, this is the last week. Akana hopes you now have a plan for one piece of patient effort of your own, with steps and a date to review. That is the use Smiles had in mind.

titles.card_line: Try Mason's outdoor hours, short lessons and narration at home.
titles.end_state: You will have read selections from Charlotte Mason's Home Education, first published in 1886, and tried three of her ideas at home. These are outdoor time, short lessons and narration, where a child tells back what they have heard. You will have kept brief notes on what happened and what you would change. By week eight you will have a small routine for your own family that borrows what suits you. Akana wrote the exercises. The book is Mason's.
who_for: Parents and carers interested in home education
Teachers curious about a nineteenth century method
Anyone who wants a short list of ideas to try at home

letters.title: A note from Akana about Charlotte M. Mason
letters.body: {first_name}, welcome. This note is from Akana, about Charlotte Mason. Her book Home Education was first published in 1886, and parents still read it today. Akana has chosen selections and written the exercises. The ideas are hers.

letters.title: A note from Akana, week 2
letters.body: {first_name}, outdoor time is the first idea. Try a regular hour outside with your child and keep a short note of what you both noticed. Akana asks only that you try it and write down what happens.

letters.title: A note from Akana, week 4
letters.body: {first_name}, short lessons come next. Mason favoured brief, focused sessions with full attention. Try one or two, and note how your child responds. Adapt freely to your own household.

letters.title: A note from Akana, week 6
letters.body: {first_name}, narration asks a child to tell back what they have heard. It sounds simple. Listen to it as a way of seeing what stayed with them, and write down what you notice.

letters.title: A note from Akana, week 8
letters.body: {first_name}, this is the last week. Akana hopes you have a small routine for your own family that borrows what suits you. Mason wrote for her time, and you are free to adapt her ideas to yours.

titles.card_line: Read one book of the Meditations a week and keep a daily reflection.
titles.end_state: You will have read the Meditations, one book a week for twelve weeks, in George Long's 1862 translation, lightly modernised. Each week brings a short account of the book, key ideas with examples, and two exercises for your own notebook. By the end you will have a reflection written for each book and a short page of the ideas you chose to keep. Akana wrote the guides and exercises. The words of Marcus Aurelius are his, as Long translated them.
who_for: Readers who want to take their time with a classic
Anyone curious about Stoic ideas in plain language
People who like to think with a notebook

letters.title: A note from Akana about Marcus Aurelius
letters.body: {first_name}, welcome. This note is from Akana, about Marcus Aurelius. The Meditations are private notes written by a Roman emperor nearly two thousand years ago. Akana has written the guides and exercises. His words are quoted as George Long translated them.

letters.title: A note from Akana, week 3
letters.body: {first_name}, you are three books in. The emperor wrote these notes for himself, and they repeat and return to the same themes. Read them slowly. Akana suggests choosing one line each week to carry through your days.

letters.title: A note from Akana, week 6
letters.body: {first_name}, you are halfway. Look back at your notebook. Which ideas have stayed with you, and which have faded? Both answers are useful.

letters.title: A note from Akana, week 9
letters.body: {first_name}, the later books are harder and darker in places. Akana asks you to read them at your own pace. Skip a passage if you wish, and return another day.

letters.title: A note from Akana, week 12
letters.body: {first_name}, this is the last week. Akana hopes you now have a notebook of your own reflections and a short page of the ideas you chose to keep. The book is the emperor's. The page is yours.

titles.card_line: Use Bennett's plan for the hours outside work, one evening at a time.
titles.end_state: You will have read Arnold Bennett's short book, first published in 1908. You will have tried his plan for the hours outside work, one evening at a time. You will have kept a simple record of an ordinary day. You will have chosen a small amount of time to give to something you care about. By week six you will have a modest weekly plan of your own and a date to review it. Akana wrote the exercises. The book is Bennett's.
who_for: People who feel the day slips away after work
Readers who like short, brisk books from the early twentieth century
Anyone ready to try a small, steady plan

letters.title: A note from Akana about Arnold Bennett
letters.body: {first_name}, welcome. This note is from Akana, about Arnold Bennett. His short book appeared in 1908 and argued that the hours outside work are the ones to use well. Akana has added exercises. The ideas are his.

letters.title: A note from Akana, week 2
letters.body: {first_name}, the first exercises ask you to record how an ordinary day is spent. This is a record, not a test. Write down what you find without judging it.

letters.title: A note from Akana, week 4
letters.body: {first_name}, Bennett suggests giving a small, regular amount of time to something you care about. Akana asks you to try that on a few evenings. Write down what you chose and how it went.

letters.title: A note from Akana, week 6
letters.body: {first_name}, this is the last week. Akana hopes you now have a modest weekly plan and a date to review it. Bennett's book is over a century old, and the plan is yours.
